summary:
Background

Retatrutide, an investigational triple agonist of glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon-like peptide 1, and glucagon receptors, may be useful for treating obstructive sleep apnea (OSA).

Methods

In two phase 3, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials nested within larger basket trials of once-weekly subcutaneous retatrutide, we assigned adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and a body-mass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) of at least 27, without (TRIUMPH-1-OSA) or with (TRIUMPH-2-OSA) type 2 diabetes, to receive retatrutide (4, 9, or 12 mg) or placebo. The primary end point was the change in the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI, the average number of apneas and hypopneas per hour of sleep) at 80 weeks with 9 mg and 12 mg of retatrutide. For OSA-related end points, a hybrid-treatment estimand was applied, with a hypothetical strategy used for participants who had intercurrent events suggesting treatment failure and a treatment-policy strategy used elsewhere. We also report intention-to-treat (ITT) results.

Results

A total of 243 participants underwent randomization in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and 448 in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. The baseline mean AHI was 58.6 and 55.9 events per hour, respectively, and the mean body weight was 119.6 and 115.9 kg. At 80 weeks, the mean changes in the AHI (hybrid-treatment estimand) with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-1-OSA were -22.9 (4 mg), -34.3 (9 mg), and -31.7 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -9.9 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -13.0 [95% confidence interval {CI}, -23.0 to -3.0], -24.4 [95% CI, -34.1 to -14.7], and -21.9 [95% CI, -32.2 to -11.5], respectively). The changes with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-2-OSA were -19.2 (4 mg), -24.7 (9 mg), and -25.4 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -10.3 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -8.9 [95% CI, -15.9 to -2.0], -14.4 [95% CI, -21.6 to -7.2], and -15.1 [95% CI, -22.5 to -7.7]). For the ITT estimand, the corresponding differences from placebo were -13.2 (95% CI, -22.6 to -3.9), -24.7 (95% CI, -34.1 to -15.3), and -22.5 (95% CI, -31.9 to -13.1) in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and -8.8 (95% CI, -15.8 to -1.7), -13.9 (95% CI, -21.3 to -6.6), and -15.0 (95% CI, -22.5 to -7.4) in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. The mean percent change in body weight with retatrutide (key secondary end point) was -12.5 to -22.2% in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and -12.1 to -18.5% in TRIUMPH-2-OSA, versus -4.8% and -5.6% with placebo (treatment-regimen estimand). The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal.

Conclusions

In adults with OSA and obesity or overweight with or without type 2 diabetes, retatrutide resulted in significantly greater decreases in the AHI than placebo. (Funded by Eli Lilly; TRIUMPH-1 and -2 ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT05929066 and NCT05929079.).
title: Retatrutide Once Weekly for Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea.

summary:
Background

B-cell activating factor (BAFF) and a proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL) have distinct roles in IgA-producing B-cell populations and appear to be central to the pathogenesis of IgA nephropathy. Povetacicept, an enhanced, variant transmembrane activator and calcium-modulator and cyclophilin-ligand interactor (TACI)-Fc fragment fusion therapeutic, is engineered for dual inhibition of BAFF and APRIL.

Methods

In this ongoing, phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, participants with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy receiving stable background therapy were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive povetacicept at a dose of 80 mg or placebo subcutaneously every 4 weeks. The primary end point of this prespecified interim analysis was the change in the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at week 36. Secondary end points were the change at week 36 in galactose-deficient IgA1 levels and hematuria resolution at week 36 among participants with baseline hematuria.

Results

A total of 557 participants received povetacicept (372 participants) or placebo (185 participants). Efficacy analyses included the first 199 participants who had undergone randomization (131 in the povetacicept group and 68 in the placebo group). The 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio decreased by 52.0% with povetacicept and by 4.3% with placebo by week 36 (adjusted difference, -49.8 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -58.6 to -39.2; P<0.001). Galactose-deficient IgA1 levels decreased by 77.4% with povetacicept and increased by 9.1% with placebo (adjusted difference, -79.3 percentage points; 95% CI, -82.2 to -75.9; P<0.001). Among the participants with baseline hematuria, resolution occurred in 85% with povetacicept and in 23% with placebo (adjusted difference, 62 percentage points; 95% CI, 45 to 78; P<0.001). The incidence of adverse events (75% with povetacicept and 78% with placebo) and serious adverse events (3% and 4%, respectively) were similar in the trial groups.

Conclusions

Povetacicept led to a significantly greater reduction in the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio than placebo by week 36 in participants with IgA nephropathy. (Funded by Vertex Pharmaceuticals; RAINIER AIS-D08 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06564142.).
title: Interim Analysis of a Phase 3 Trial of Povetacicept in IgA Nephropathy.

summary:
Background

Neoadjuvant immune checkpoint blockade induces high pathological response rates in patients with locally advanced mismatch repair-deficient (dMMR) colon cancer, yet long-term survival outcomes have not been established. Previously, we reported safety (a primary endpoint) and pathological response (a secondary endpoint) data from the NICHE-2 trial. Here, we report the primary efficacy endpoint of 3-year disease-free survival and the exploratory endpoint of 5-year overall survival.

Methods

In this single-arm, multicentre, phase 2, NICHE-2 trial, patients with previously untreated, clinical stage 2 or 3, resectable dMMR colon cancer received a single dose of intravenous ipilimumab (1 mg per kg) on day 1, and two doses of intravenous nivolumab (3 mg per kg) on days 1 and 15, followed by surgery in one of the six participating hospitals in the Netherlands. Here, we report the independent primary efficacy endpoint of 3-year disease-free survival (time from surgery until disease recurrence or death from any cause) and the secondary endpoint of circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) analysis. Overall survival (time from study enrolment until death from any cause) is reported as an exploratory post-hoc analysis. All endpoints were assessed in the per-protocol population (patients who met the eligibility criteria and received at least one cycle of therapy). The study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03026140, and has completed accrual.

Findings

From July 4, 2017, to July 18, 2022, 123 patients were screened, of whom 115 were treated and 111 were included in the per-protocol population. At the data cutoff (June 19, 2026), the postoperative median follow-up was 58·7 months (IQR 49·0-72·9). The 3-year disease-free survival was 100% (97·5% CI 100-100). After a median follow-up of 60·4 months (IQR 50·6-74·1), calculated from time of study enrolment, the 5-year overall survival was 100% (95% CI 100-100). In patients with available plasma samples, ctDNA was detected in 99 (92%) of 108 patients at baseline, and ctDNA clearance was observed in 44 (45%) of 98 patients after the first cycle in week 2 and in 80 (82%) of 97 patients after the second cycle before surgery. In patients with a pathological near-complete response and complete response, presurgery ctDNA clearance was observed in 19 (70%) of 27 patients and 60 (92%) of 65 patients, respectively. Assessment for minimal residual disease after surgery revealed that all patients were ctDNA negative.

Interpretation

In patients with locally advanced dMMR colon cancer, treatment with ipilimumab and nivolumab before surgery resulted in a 3-year disease-free survival and 5-year overall survival of 100%. These findings support neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab as a potential standard of care for patients with locally advanced dMMR colon cancer.

Funding

Bristol Myers Squibb.
title: Disease-free survival and overall survival after neoadjuvant immunotherapy in mismatch repair-deficient colon cancer in the Netherlands: results of the single-arm, multicentre, phase 2, NICHE-2 trial.

summary:
Background

Sibeprenlimab, a humanized monoclonal antibody, selectively inhibits the cytokine A proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL), a key driver of IgA nephropathy. Preliminary trial results with regard to the primary end point of the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at 9 months after treatment as compared with baseline have been reported, but secondary end points, including outcomes regarding estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), have not.

Methods

We randomly assigned adults with IgA nephropathy to receive subcutaneous sibeprenlimab (at a dose of 400 mg) or placebo every 4 weeks. The key secondary end point was the annualized slope of the eGFR over 24 months. Other secondary end points included the change in eGFR from baseline to 24 months, a composite kidney end point of kidney-function decline or kidney failure, and pharmacodynamic and safety end points.

Results

A total of 510 patients underwent randomization - 259 to receive sibeprenlimab and 251 to receive placebo. The annualized eGFR slope over 24 months was 0.3 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area per year (95% confidence interval [CI], -0.4 to 0.9) with sibeprenlimab and -4.2 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 per year (95% CI, -4.9 to -3.6) with placebo (between-group difference, 4.5 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 per year; 95% CI, 3.6 to 5.4; P<0.001). The least-squares mean treatment difference for the change in eGFR from baseline to 24 months was 9.2 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, 7.1 to 11.4; P<0.001). A composite kidney end-point event occurred in 1 patient (0.4%) in the sibeprenlimab group and in 28 patients (11.2%) in the placebo group (adjusted difference, -10.8 percentage points; hazard ratio, 0.029; 95% CI, 0.004 to 0.214; P<0.001). Adverse events occurred in 235 patients (90.7%) in the sibeprenlimab group and 226 patients (90.0%) in the placebo group; serious adverse events occurred in 21 patients (8.1%) and 32 patients (12.7%), respectively; and serious infections in 5 patients (1.9%) and 10 patients (4.0%). No deaths were reported.

Conclusions

Among patients with IgA nephropathy, treatment with sibeprenlimab stabilized the eGFR slope over 24 months, a finding consistent with a reduced risk of kidney-function decline. (Funded by Otsuka Pharmaceutical Development and Commercialization; VISIONARY ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05248646.).
title: Sibeprenlimab in IgA Nephropathy - Final Phase 3 Trial Analysis.

summary:
Importance

Trastuzumab rezetecan (SHR-A1811) has demonstrated encouraging antitumor activity in a global phase 1 trial involving heavily pretreated patients with erythroblastic oncogene B (ERBB2)-low metastatic breast cancer.

Objective

To compare trastuzumab rezetecan vs physician's choice of chemotherapy in patients with ERBB2-low metastatic breast cancer.

Design, setting, and participants

This open-label, randomized, multicenter phase 3 trial was conducted at 73 hospitals across China. Eligible patients were females aged 18 to 75 years with centrally confirmed ERBB2-low (immunohistochemistry [IHC] 1+ or IHC 2+/in-situ hybridization [ISH]-negative) unresectable locally recurrent or metastatic breast cancer who had received 1 or fewer prior lines of chemotherapy for metastatic disease, with prior endocrine therapy required for hormone receptor-positive disease. Enrollment began on June 30, 2023, and ended on August 20, 2025. The last day of follow-up for the final analysis for progression-free survival in the current study was March 20, 2026.

Interventions

Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive trastuzumab rezetecan (6.4 mg/kg intravenously every 3 weeks; n = 277) or physician's choice of chemotherapy (n = 274).

Main outcomes and measures

The primary end point was progression-free survival assessed by blinded independent central review in chemotherapy-naive patients and the overall population.

Results

Between June 30, 2023, and August 20, 2025, a total of 551 patients were randomized, with a mean (SD) age of 54.9 (9.9) years. At the data cutoff (March 20, 2026), trastuzumab rezetecan significantly prolonged progression-free survival compared with chemotherapy in the chemotherapy-naive patients (median, 16.6 [95% CI, 14.0-19.4] months vs 6.8 [95% CI, 5.7-7.0] months; hazard ratio, 0.25 [95% CI, 0.19-0.33]; P < .001) and the overall population (median, 16.4 [95% CI, 14.0-16.8] months vs 6.8 [95% CI, 5.7-6.9] months; hazard ratio, 0.27 [95% CI, 0.21-0.34]; P < .001). The benefit was consistent in hormone receptor-negative disease (median progression-free survival: 16.5 vs 6.8 months; hazard ratio, 0.34, [95% CI, 0.22-0.54]) and hormone receptor-positive disease (median progression-free survival: 16.4 vs 6.7 months; hazard ratio, 0.24 [95% CI, 0.18-0.33]). Grade 3 or greater treatment-related adverse events occurred in 84.1% of patients (232/276) with trastuzumab rezetecan and 67.9% (184/271) with chemotherapy, most commonly decreased neutrophil count (180 [65.2%] vs 147 [54.2%]).

Conclusions and relevance

Trastuzumab rezetecan provided significant progression-free survival benefit over physician's choice of chemotherapy in patients with ERBB2-low advanced breast cancer, with benefit observed across all key subgroups. It exhibited the potential as a new treatment option with a distinct safety profile in this setting.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05814354.
title: Trastuzumab Rezetecan in ERBB2-Low Advanced Breast Cancer: The HORIZON-Breast06 Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary:
Background

In patients with IgA nephropathy, complement activation drives glomerular inflammation, which leads to hematuria, proteinuria, and nephron loss. Ravulizumab is a terminal complement inhibitor that prevents formation of C5a and C5b-9.

Methods

In this phase 3 trial, we enrolled adults with IgA nephropathy who had an estimated glomerular filtration rate of at least 30 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area and proteinuria (24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio [with protein and creatinine both measured in grams] of ≥0.75 or total urinary protein excretion of ≥1.0 g per day), despite standard therapy. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive an intravenous infusion of either ravulizumab or placebo every 8 weeks. In the prespecified interim analysis, the primary efficacy end point was the change from baseline in the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at week 34. Safety was also assessed.

Results

In all, 485 patients underwent randomization, with 240 patients assigned to the ravulizumab group and 245 to the placebo group; 352 patients (176 in each group) were included in the interim analysis. In the ravulizumab group, the geometric mean 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at baseline and at week 34 was 1.56 and 0.83, respectively; in the placebo group, it was 1.60 and 1.48, respectively. At week 34, a significant reduction in the geometric mean 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio was observed with ravulizumab (-46.6%) as compared with the reduction observed with placebo (-5.6%), corresponding to an adjusted geometric mean 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio that was 43.4% (99% confidence interval, 30.1 to 54.2) lower with ravulizumab than with placebo (P<0.001). Adverse events occurred in 69.5% of the patients receiving ravulizumab and in 75.8% of those receiving placebo; serious adverse events occurred in 4.6% and 9.0%, respectively. No meningococcal infections or deaths occurred.

Conclusions

In adults with IgA nephropathy, ravulizumab resulted in a significantly greater reduction in the protein-to-creatinine ratio than placebo at week 34. (Funded by Alexion, AstraZeneca Rare Disease Unit; I CAN ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06291376; EU Clinical Trials number, 2023-507851-31-00.).

summary:
Background

Trifluridine-tipiracil (FTD-TPI) plus bevacizumab is the standard treatment for refractory metastatic colorectal cancer. However, the conventional schedule is frequently associated with haematological and gastrointestinal toxicity, which is clinically significant and relevant to patients. A simplified 14-day schedule has been proposed to reduce toxicity, but whether this treatment preserves survival has not been established in a randomised trial. We therefore aimed to assess whether the 14-day schedule is non-inferior to the conventional schedule for overall survival.

Methods

PRABITAS was a pragmatic, multicentre, open-label, randomised, phase 3, non-inferiority trial conducted in 178 hospitals in Japan. Patients with refractory metastatic colorectal cancer were randomly assigned (1:1) using a minimisation algorithm, stratified by Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status, RAS mutational status, and institution, to FTD-TPI (35 mg/m2 orally twice daily) plus bevacizumab (5 mg/kg intravenously) on either a conventional 28-day (FTD-TPI on days 1-5 and 8-12; bevacizumab on days 1 and 15) or 14-day schedule (FTD-TPI on days 1-5; bevacizumab on day 1). Eligibility criteria were broadened compared with those of conventional explanatory trials, and trial procedures were aligned with routine clinical practice. The primary endpoint was overall survival, analysed in the intention-to-treat population, with a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 1·25. Safety was assessed in all patients who received at least one dose. Missing data were not imputed. This trial is registered with the Japan Registry of Clinical Trials, jRCTs041230120, and is closed to enrolment.

Findings

Between Dec 26, 2023, and May 20, 2025, we randomly assigned 972 patients, of whom 970 (99%) constituted the intention-to-treat population after two were excluded because they were randomly assigned before site approval (486 [50%] to the 28-day treatment group, 292 [60%] men and 194 [40%] women]; and 484 [50%] to the 14-day treatment group, 264 [55%] men and 220 [45%] women). Median follow-up was 17·9 months (IQR 14·3-22·6). Median overall survival was 10·3 months (95% CI 9·5-11·6) in the 28-day group and 11·3 months (10·2-12·5) in the 14-day group (stratified hazard ratio 0·93 [95% CI 0·80-1·08]). The 12-month overall survival rates were 44·0% (95% CI 39·5-48·5) in the 28-day group and 47·5% (42·9-52·0) in the 14-day group. Neutropenia grade 3 or worse was reduced in the 14-day group (13% vs 39%; absolute difference 25 percentage points [95% CI 20-31]), as was anorexia grade 2 or worse (15% vs 26%; absolute difference 11 percentage points [6-16]). Two treatment-related deaths occurred in the 14-day group and none in the 28-day group.

Interpretation

A 14-day schedule of FTD-TPI plus bevacizumab was non-inferior to the conventional 28-day schedule for overall survival, while reducing haematological and gastrointestinal toxicity. These findings support this simplified schedule as the new standard for FTD-TPI plus bevacizumab in refractory metastatic colorectal cancer.

Funding

Japan Society for the Promotion of Science KAKENHI Grant-in-Aid for Challenging Research (Pioneering).
title: 14-day versus 28-day trifluridine-tipiracil plus bevacizumab for refractory metastatic colorectal cancer (PRABITAS): a pragmatic, multicentre, open-label, randomised, phase 3, non-inferiority trial in Japan.

summary: Exchange Pre-Eligibility Verification Proposed Rule (CMS 9873-P) Introduction Consistent with the President’s goal to prevent waste, fraud, and abuse, today the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), issued the Exchange Pre-Eligibility Verification Notice of Proposed Rulemaking. This rule would align Exchange eligibility and verification regulations with new requirements specified under the Working Families Tax Cuts (WFTC) legislation (P.L. 119-21). The WFTC legislation amended the Internal Revenue Code to establish new eligibility requirements for the premium tax credit (PTC). The Exchange Pre-Eligibility Verification proposed rule would establish new Exchange requirements that align advance payments of the premium tax credit (APTC) and cost-sharing reductions (CSRs) eligibility with PTC eligibility changes enacted under sec. 71303 of the WFTC legislation and proposed to be codified in regulations issued by the Department of the Treasury on October 15, 2026. Currently, when consumers apply for coverage through Exchanges, they provide certain information that Exchanges may attempt to verify electronically. If an Exchange cannot verify the information electronically, the consumer enters an inconsistency period during which they need to submit documentation to verify their information. Under existing policy established by the Affordable Care Act (ACA), Exchanges provide APTC and CSRs (collectively, financial assistance) during the inconsistency period to consumers who otherwise appear eligible. If they do not submit documentation to verify their eligibility before the end of the inconsistency period, APTC and CSRs are generally reduced or ended. The Exchange Pre-Eligibility Verification proposed rule would require Exchanges to verify the following criteria before providing financial assistance: household income and family size status as a citizen, U.S. national, or eligible noncitizen (including lawfully present) eligibility for or enrollment in other qualifying coverage place of residence However, under the proposed rule, consumers could enroll in Exchange coverage without financial assistance during the inconsistency period while verifications are pending. It would also establish a verification period beginning August 1 before Open Enrollment (OE) each year to ensure that consumers have ample opportunity to provide and confirm information impacting their eligibility before the following coverage year. This proposed rule also includes provisions on annual eligibility redeterminations and re-enrollment, eligibility redeterminations during the plan year, timeline requirements for states seeking to transition to a State-based Exchange, binder payments, a waiver of the proposed verification requirements for certain Special Enrollment Periods (SEPs), effective dates for eligibility determinations, annual OE notices, and plan selection requirements. The proposed regulations would ensure financial assistance is only provided when income can be verified, potentially reducing the risk that consumers would have to repay excess APTC at tax filing due to inaccurate income estimates. They also would reduce improper or fraudulent enrollments by requiring verification of certain eligibility criteria before providing financial assistance, improving program integrity. The provisions in the Exchange Pre-Eligibility Verification proposed rule would be effective starting with eligibility determinations made for plan year 2028. The rule would require Exchanges to make a pre-OE verification period available starting August 1 each year ahead of OE, during which consumers could choose to provide eligibility verification information earlier for next coverage year. The first pre-OE window would start August 1, 2027, for 2028 coverage. The Exchange Pre-Eligibility Verification proposed rule is available on the Federal Register at: https://www.federalregister.gov/public-inspection/2026-21891/patient-protection-and-affordable-care-act-exchange-pre-eligibility-verification . Stakeholders may submit public comments for a 30-day period following publication of the proposed rule. Strengthening Program Integrity Requiring Verification Before Receiving Financial Assistance CMS proposes new regulations for verification requirements for consumers requesting financial assistance for Exchange coverage. Exchanges would no longer be permitted to provide financial assistance during inconsistency periods when certain eligibility criteria cannot be verified electronically. Additionally, CMS proposes that Exchanges maintain or reduce the amount of financial assistance provided during such inconsistency periods after an enrollee voluntarily reports a change in circumstances that impacts eligibility for financial help. These new requirements would help ensure that only eligible consumers receive financial assistance. Requiring Annual Verification CMS proposes that currently enrolled consumers would only be automatically re-enrolled with financial assistance if they return to the Exchange to confirm certain eligibility criteria annually and have it re-verified by the Exchange. Consumers who don't actively return and have their information re-verified for financial help would be automatically re-enrolled without financial assistance. The new requirement would help ensure that only eligible consumers receive financial assistance through annual re-enrollment. Supporting Exchange Consumers Opportunity for Verification Before Open Enrollment Beginning August 1, 2027, CMS proposes that Exchanges provide consumers the option to submit certain eligibility information for the Exchange to verify before annual OE. CMS proposes requiring all Exchanges make this pre-OE verification period available to new and returning applicants to provide a minimum set of eligibility information and that all Exchanges start their annual pre-OE verification period on August 1 each year. By providing the early opportunity for verification, the proposed rule would help Exchange enrollees to have their eligibility fully verified before the upcoming coverage year, ensuring continuous coverage with financial assistance from year to year. Flexible Enrollment Options for Consumers CMS proposes requiring Exchanges to allow consumers to select a contingent plan during OE or a SEP such that the plan selection would become effective only if the consumer is determined eligible for financial assistance. This means consumers may choose a plan based on preliminary financial assistance estimates that would only start after they confirm eligibility for financial assistance. This process would enable consumers who elect not to enroll when they do not receive financial assistance during their inconsistency period to enroll once they are determined eligible for financial assistance, even if OE or their SEP, as applicable, has ended. Ensuring Timely Access to Financial Assistance CMS proposes new effective date rules for eligibility determinations and redeterminations made under the other proposed requirements in this rule. These proposals include new effective dates for financial assistance eligibility determinations and redeterminations after successful verification of eligibility. For consumers already enrolled in a health plan when their eligibility for financial assistance is verified, we propose providing financial assistance retroactively for the months during their inconsistency period when they were enrolled. For consumers who select a plan pending verification of eligibility for financial assistance, meaning the plan won’t start until after verification, we propose that their enrollment and financial assistance become effective and will start based on when their eligibility is verified. These proposed rules would provide clarity to consumers, Exchanges, and issuers; ensure timely access to coverage and financial assistance; and limit risks of adverse selection. Flexibility in Open Enrollment Notification Starting with plan year 2028, CMS proposes to permit Exchanges to provide the written annual OE notification to each enrollee before the pre-OE verification period, instead of in the month before OE starts. This would permit Exchanges to design the most effective outreach strategy to educate their consumers about the earlier verification period opportunity and the annual OE. Exception for Changes in Family Size CMS proposes waiving new verification requirements for consumers with certain changes in family size, as outlined in Treasury’s regulations, so that their financial assistance is based on their attested application information during inconsistency periods. This applies when a consumer or their household member qualifies for an SEP triggered by birth, adoption, marriage, or loss of a dependent through divorce, separation, or death (if allowed by the Exchange). Improving Exchange Rules Comment Solicitation on Enhancing Verification Procedures CMS seeks comment on how to strengthen Exchange requirements to verify family size and residency, including which data sources CMS should consider using or making available. CMS seeks comment on ways to increase program integrity while limiting burden on consumers and limiting operational costs and burdens for state and federal Exchanges. State Exchange Transitions CMS proposes that a state submits its application for HHS’ review and approval to become a State-based Exchange 15 months before a state begins operations as a State Exchange for the pre-OE verification period, instead of 15 months before OE. This would ensure the required pre-OE verification period is available to consumers when a State-based Exchange launches, removing the risk that a consumer first verifies on the Federally-facilitated Exchange (FFE) during the pre-OE verification period and then must reverify on the State-based Exchange. This requirement would ensure transitioning states align their transition timeline with the start of the pre-OE verification period, which would be the start of their operations as a State-based Exchange, instead of the start of OE. Binder Payment Alignment CMS proposes that the FFE and State-based Exchanges on the Federal Platform (SBE-FPs) must make prospective and retroactive enrollments under this proposed rule subject to the existing binder payment rules for prospective and retroactive enrollments, respectively. In addition, State-based Exchanges have the option to adopt the same changes. This would give issuers additional flexibility to set binder payment due dates for the proposed new enrollment scenarios. Effective Dates CMS proposes limited updates for current rules on effective dates for financial assistance eligibility redeterminations, when an existing enrollee reports a change to the Exchange during the coverage year. Specifically, in cases where the enrollee does not qualify for an SEP, CMS proposes no longer allowing Exchanges to delay effective dates for such eligibility redeterminations beyond the first of the month after the redetermination occurs. This change would align effective dates across existing and new scenarios and ensure timely eligibility updates. CMS News and Media Group Catherine Howden, Director Media Inquiries Form 202-690-6145

summary:
Objective

To assess the added value of acetic acid chromoendoscopy (AAC) for the detection of dysplasia and oesophageal adenocarcinoma during Barrett's oesophagus surveillance endoscopies.

Design

Prospective, open label, stepped wedge cluster, randomised trial.

Setting

18 Dutch community hospitals.

Participants

Patients undergoing surveillance for Barrett's oesophagus were eligible, excluding those with known or previously treated dysplasia.

Interventions

Hospitals randomly shifted from surveillance without AAC (control) to AAC (intervention), with endoscopists trained before implementation. Targeted biopsies were obtained if lesions were present; random four quadrant biopsies were conducted.

Main outcome measures

The primary endpoint was the neoplasia detection rate, defined as the percentage of participants with low grade dysplasia, high grade dysplasia, and oesophageal adenocarcinoma in any biopsy, confirmed by an experienced gastrointestinal pathologist. The secondary endpoint was the neoplasia detection rate in targeted biopsies.

Results

2267 participants were included, of whom 1438 (63%) were allocated to surveillance without AAC and 829 (37%) to surveillance with AAC; AAC was applied in 679 (82%) allocated participants. Overall, neoplasia was diagnosed in 163 (7.2%) participants (111 (4.9%) low grade dysplasia, 30 (1.3%) high grade dysplasia, and 22 (1.0%) oesophageal adenocarcinoma). AAC use did not increase the neoplasia detection rate (7.4% (50/679) with AAC versus 7.1% (113/1588) without AAC; odds ratio 0.97, 95% confidence interval 0.65 to 1.44; adjusted for calendar time and Barrett's oesophagus length). Suspected lesions were detected in 95 (14.0%) participants receiving AAC versus 101 (6.4%) without AAC (P<0.001), but the targeted neoplasia detection rate was not higher (2.1% (14/679) versus 1.8% (29/1588); odds ratio 1.05, 0.49 to 2.24).

Conclusions

Use of AAC did not improve detection of neoplasia in patients with Barrett's oesophagus undergoing endoscopic surveillance in routine clinical practice.

Trial registration

www.onderzoekmetmensen.nl; NL-OMON25059 (prospective registration; 4 Dec 2019).
title: Acetic acid chromoendoscopy for detection of neoplastic Barrett's oesophagus: stepped wedge cluster randomised controlled trial (ACID-trial).

summary:
Background

Remibrutinib is a highly selective, potent, covalent, CNS-penetrant, oral BTK inhibitor. We assessed the efficacy and safety of remibrutinib in adult patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis.

Methods

REMODEL-1 and REMODEL-2 are two identical, randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, active comparator-controlled, parallel-group, event-driven, phase 3 trials conducted at 407 centres in 46 countries. Patients aged 18-55 years with relapsing multiple sclerosis, an Expanded Disability Status Scale score of 0-5·5, and evidence of recent disease activity were randomly assigned 1:1 to oral remibrutinib 100 mg twice daily or teriflunomide 14 mg once daily via interactive response technology. Randomisation was stratified by geographical region, MRI cohort participation, and multiple sclerosis subtype. Patients, site investigators, and trial team were masked to treatment allocation. The primary endpoint was annualised relapse rate (ARR), defined as the number of confirmed multiple sclerosis relapses per patient-year with up to 30 months of follow-up, and assessed in all randomly assigned patients. These trials are registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05147220 and NCT05156281) and are ongoing, not recruiting.

Findings

Between Dec 13, 2021, and Dec 30, 2025, 2632 patients were screened and 2007 patients were randomly assigned. REMODEL-1 included 1000 patients (remibrutinib 502, teriflunomide 498; mean age 38·2 years, 666 [66·6%] female, 334 [33·4%] male) and REMODEL-2 included 1007 patients (remibrutinib 504, teriflunomide 503; mean age 39·0 years, 675 [67·0%] female, 332 [33·0%] male). ARR was significantly lower with remibrutinib than with teriflunomide: 0·073 versus 0·112 (rate ratio [RR] 0·648 [95% CI 0·453-0·927]; p=0·018) in REMODEL-1 and 0·080 versus 0·116 (RR 0·688 [0·487-0·972]; p=0·034) in REMODEL-2. The most common adverse events were upper respiratory tract infection (132 [13·1%] of 1006 with remibrutinib vs 137 [13·7%] of 1001 with teriflunomide), nasopharyngitis (92 [9·1%] vs 123 [12·3%]), diarrhoea (84 [8·3%] vs 109 [10·9%]), and alopecia (58 [5·8%] vs 135 [13·5%]). Adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation were less frequent with remibrutinib (31 [3·1%]) versus teriflunomide (58 [5·8%]). The safety profile of remibrutinib was consistent with that in other indications, including no liver safety concerns.

Interpretation

Remibrutinib was superior to teriflunomide in patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis, while maintaining a favourable safety profile. These findings support remibrutinib as a potential new oral treatment option for relapsing multiple sclerosis.

Funding

Novartis.
title: Remibrutinib versus teriflunomide in relapsing multiple sclerosis (REMODEL-1 and REMODEL-2): two randomised, phase 3 trials.

summary:
Background

The United States recently proposed changes to the recommendations for childhood hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination.

Objective

To project the effect of vaccine policy changes, if fully implemented, on chronic HBV infections.

Design

Markov cohort state transition model of perinatal and childhood HBV infection.

Data sources

Published data on maternal HBV prevalence (0.4%) and hepatitis B surface antigen testing (99.5% sensitivity), childhood vaccine completion (universal birth-dose strategy: 91.1%; deferred strategy: 87.1%; shared decision-making strategy: 50.0%), and age-stratified risk for chronic HBV infection.

Target population

One-year birth cohort of U.S.-born infants (n = 3.6 million).

Time horizon

20 years.

Intervention

Universal birth-dose vaccination, deferred (2-month) vaccination, and vaccination through shared decision making.

Outcome measures

Numbers with chronic HBV infection and susceptibility to HBV, with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs) derived from probabilistic sensitivity analysis.

Results of base-case analysis

Compared with the universal birth-dose strategy (255 childhood infections [95% UI, 130 to 530]), the deferred and shared decision-making strategies would increase chronic HBV infections in the 2026 birth cohort by 19% to 303 (95% UI, 155 to 610) and by 83% to 467 (95% UI, 209 to 1032), respectively. These strategies would also increase the number of HBV-susceptible people at year 20 (474 000 and 1 806 000) compared with the universal birth-dose strategy (232 000).

Results of sensitivity analysis

In a scenario with lower vaccine coverage (84.5%) and higher HBV prevalence (maternal prevalence of 0.72% and higher risk for horizontal infection), chronic HBV infections would increase to 1700 and 2192, respectively, with the deferred and shared decision-making strategies.

Limitation

Uncertainty in horizontal HBV infection risk.

Conclusion

Proposed policy changes for vaccination through shared decision making are projected to result in an 83% increase in childhood HBV infections, and between 50% and 70% of children entering adulthood annually would be susceptible to HBV infection. Policymakers should reimplement recommendations for universal birth-dose vaccination.

Primary funding source

summary:
Importance

For patients with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), guidelines recommend considering maintenance therapy after achieving remission. Data comparing maintenance therapeutic options are limited.

Objective

To compare the effects of rituximab and azathioprine maintenance therapies on remission duration for patients with EGPA who recently achieved remission of vasculitis after standard therapy, including prednisone tapering or withdrawal.

Design, setting, and participants

From March 7, 2018, to June 2, 2022, this double-blind, double-dummy, investigator-initiated, superiority, randomized clinical trial enrolled 98 participants with EGPA from 36 hospitals in France. Inclusion eligibility required a new EGPA diagnosis or relapsing EGPA within 30 to 360 days of achieving vasculitis remission (Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score of 0 [range, 0-63, with higher scores indicating more severe disease activity]) after a standard induction regimen. Data were analyzed from April 1, 2025, to September 17, 2025. Additional analyses ended June 22, 2026.

Interventions

Participants were randomized to receive a predefined standardized tapering of oral prednisone and either 500 mg of intravenous rituximab every 6 months for 18 months and daily oral azathioprine placebo for 24 months (n = 49) or rituximab placebo every 6 months for 18 months and daily oral azathioprine for 24 months (n = 49).

Main outcomes and measures

The primary efficacy end point was the duration of total remission during the 28-month study period while taking 7.5 mg/d or less of prednisone. The 14 secondary end points included proportion of participants remaining in remission, rate of vasculitis relapse, and rate of asthma or rhinosinusitis exacerbations.

Results

All 98 randomized participants (mean age, 59.0 years [SD, 14.4]; 50 women [51%]) received at least 1 dose of the trial regimen and 92 (94%) completed the trial. The mean time in remission with prednisone at 7.5 mg/d or less was 91.1 weeks (95% CI, 80.9-101.2) vs 96.0 weeks (95% CI, 85.6-106.5) in the rituximab and azathioprine groups, respectively (P = .38). The proportion of participants who remained in remission during the 28-month study period with prednisone at 7.5 mg/d or less was 17 of 49 (34.7%) vs 11 of 49 (22.4%; relative risk, 1.51; 95% CI, 0.83-2.73; P = .18) in the rituximab and azathioprine groups, respectively. The proportion of participants with at least 1 vasculitis relapse was 7 (14.3%) vs 9 (18.4%) in the rituximab vs azathioprine groups, respectively, and for those with at least 1 clinically significant asthma exacerbation, rhinosinusitis exacerbation, or both, it was 16 (32.7%) vs 19 (38.8%). One participant in the azathioprine group died of SARS-CoV-2 infection before vaccine development. Rituximab recipients experienced a higher incidence of severe infections (23 [46.9%] vs 12 [24.5%], respectively), primarily due to severe SARS-CoV-2 infections.

Conclusions and relevance

For participants with newly diagnosed or relapsing EGPA, rituximab was not superior to azathioprine for improving the duration of total remission during 28 months while taking prednisone at 7.5 mg/d or less.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03164473.
title: Rituximab vs Azathioprine for Eosinophilic Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis Maintenance Therapy: A Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary:
Background

Medicare Advantage insurers conduct in-home health risk assessments (HRAs) to identify high-risk patients and facilitate appropriate care. Critics argue this practice increases risk-adjusted payments without improving quality. Comprehensive data on use of in-home HRAs and downstream treatment are lacking.

Objective

To examine trends in cardiovascular conditions diagnosed during in-home HRAs, characteristics associated with HRA-based diagnoses, and treatment rates after diagnoses.

Design

Cohort study.

Setting

Population-based.

Participants

Medicare Advantage beneficiaries.

Measurements

Using 100% Medicare claims, trends in the proportion of cardiovascular conditions diagnosed during in-home HRAs (vs. facility-based visits) were examined. Multivariable logistic regression models were fit to estimate the association between beneficiary- and plan-level characteristics and HRA-based diagnoses and compare treatment rates across settings.

Results

Among 21 496 506 Medicare Advantage beneficiaries diagnosed with a cardiovascular risk factor or disease, the proportion diagnosed during in-home HRAs increased between 2018 and 2022 for hypertension (45.9% to 47.7%), hyperlipidemia (57.8% to 66.7%), diabetes (47.8% to 51.6%), atrial fibrillation (30.0% to 36.0%), ischemic heart disease (37.2% to 41.6%), peripheral vascular disease (64.5% to 73.9%), and heart failure (34.7% to 42.6%). Racial and ethnic minority beneficiaries and those enrolled in lower-rated plans were more likely to receive HRA-based diagnoses. Treatment rates were substantially lower after HRA-based diagnoses across all conditions.

Limitations

Differences in the severity of conditions between groups could not be assessed. Prescription fills were used as a proxy for management. Observed differences in the diagnosis and treatment of conditions across encounter settings may be susceptible to unmeasured confounding.

Conclusion

Among Medicare Advantage beneficiaries, an increasingly large share of cardiovascular conditions are being diagnosed through in-home HRAs, but treatment rates after these diagnoses are consistently lower than after facility-based encounters.

Primary funding source

National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute.
title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Cardiovascular Conditions in Medicare Advantage In-Home Health Risk Assessments.

summary:
Importance

Childhood cancer risk after assisted reproductive technology (ART) remains uncertain, particularly by procedure and cancer type.

Objective

To examine associations between ART and childhood cancer overall and by ART modality and cancer type.

Design, setting, and population

Nationwide Danish cohort of 1 086 136 live-born children from 1996 to 2012, of whom 37 228 (3.4%) were conceived using ART, with follow-up through 2023.

Exposures

Maternal ART, classified as in vitro fertilization (IVF), intracytoplasmic sperm injection, or frozen embryo transfer.

Main outcomes and measures

Incident childhood cancer. Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios (HRs); Poisson models estimated incidence rates. Non-ART births were the primary reference; secondary analyses used children of women with a history of infertility and children conceived using IVF as reference groups.

Results

During a median follow-up of 20 years, 3736 cancers occurred. Compared with non-ART births (incidence rate, 18.3 per 100 000 person-years), children conceived using ART had higher cancer incidence (incidence rate, 23.6 per 100 000; HR, 1.26 [95% CI, 1.07-1.48]). Rates were higher after frozen embryo transfer (incidence rate, 41.1 per 100 000; HR, 2.18 [95% CI, 1.45-3.29]) and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (incidence rate, 27.9 per 100 000; HR, 1.48 [95% CI, 1.16-1.89]) but not IVF (incidence rate, 18.5 per 100 000; HR, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.79-1.28]). Frozen embryo transfer was associated with leukemia (incidence rate, 11.1 per 100 000; HR, 2.36 [95% CI, 1.06-5.28]), lymphomas (HR, 3.03 [95% CI, 1.13-8.12]), and soft tissue sarcomas (HR, 7.63 [95% CI, 2.82-20.62]); intracytoplasmic sperm injection was associated with lymphomas (incidence rate, 4.6 per 100 000; HR, 1.94 [95% CI, 1.07-3.54]), soft tissue sarcomas (incidence rate, 3.3 per 100 000; HR, 3.28 [95% CI, 1.54-7.00]), and central nervous system neoplasms (incidence rate, 8.2 per 100 000; HR, 1.63 [95% CI, 1.04-2.57]); no associations were observed for IVF. Findings were similar in secondary analyses using children of women with a history of infertility and children conceived using IVF as reference groups.

Conclusions and relevance

ART, particularly frozen embryo transfer and intracytoplasmic sperm injection, was associated with increased childhood cancer risk, but absolute risks were low. The consistent results in secondary analyses of children with maternal infertility history or conceived via IVF suggest that procedure-related, rather than infertility-related, factors warrant further investigation.
title: Childhood Cancer Risk After Assisted Reproductive Technology.

summary:
Background

Atacicept resulted in a significantly greater reduction in the urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio than placebo in a previously published analysis of this trial, ORIGIN 3. Final prespecified efficacy results are reported here.

Methods

We randomly assigned adults with biopsy-confirmed IgA nephropathy to receive weekly subcutaneous atacicept at a dose of 150 mg or placebo. We carried out final analyses of two secondary end points: the change in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) at week 52 and the annualized eGFR slope through week 104; additional hierarchically tested end points and safety were assessed.

Results

Of 431 patients who underwent randomization, 428 received atacicept or placebo (214 per group). At week 52, the mean change in the eGFR was -0.11 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area (95% confidence interval [CI], -1.44 to 1.22) with atacicept and -5.69 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, -7.04 to -4.35) with placebo (mean difference, 5.58 ml per minute per 1.73 m2; 95% CI, 3.68 to 7.48; P<0.001). Through week 104, the mean annualized eGFR slope was -0.60 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, -1.62 to 0.41) with atacicept and -5.60 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, -6.64 to -4.57) with placebo (difference, 5.00 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 per year; 95% CI, 3.55 to 6.45; P<0.001). Composite kidney-disease progression occurred in 11 patients (5.1%) in the atacicept group and in 38 patients (17.8%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.24; 95% CI, 0.12 to 0.48; P<0.001); no patients in the atacicept group had progression to dialysis, transplantation, or death, as compared with 7 patients in the placebo group. Adverse events occurred in 160 of 214 patients (74.8%) in the atacicept group and in 167 of 214 patients (78.0%) in the placebo group; serious adverse events occurred in 7.0% and 15.4%, respectively. One patient (in the placebo group) died.

Conclusions

Atacicept slowed and stabilized the decline in the eGFR as compared with placebo. (Funded by Vera Therapeutics; ORIGIN 3 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04716231.).
title: Atacicept in IgA Nephropathy - Phase 3 Trial Final Efficacy Analysis.

summary: Regulatory Alignment for Predictable and Immediate Device Coverage Pathway (CMS-3487-NC) Procedural Notice Inviting Comment The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a proposed procedural notice outlining a faster way for manufacturers to get new devices covered by Medicare: the Regulatory Alignment for Predictable and Immediate Device (RAPID) coverage pathway. First announced by CMS and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on April 23, 2026, this new Medicare coverage pathway will accelerate beneficiary access to eligible Class II FDA-designated Breakthrough Devices participating in FDA’s Total Product Life Cycle Advisory Program (TAP) and to eligible Class III FDA-designated Breakthrough Devices (regardless of TAP participation). Under the RAPID coverage pathway, CMS and FDA will use existing programs and coverage frameworks to analyze and approve in a more timely and predictable way those devices that demonstrate positive clinical health outcomes in the premarket phase. Specifically, RAPID leverages FDA’s existing process to assess clinical outcomes in proposed Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) studies to facilitate a more efficient and streamlined process for manufacturers seeking Medicare coverage after FDA market authorization. Through the RAPID coverage pathway, CMS will join early and frequent engagement opportunities between FDA and device manufacturers — linking manufacturers to CMS experts early in development to understand what clinical outcomes are most relevant for Medicare beneficiaries. By aligning CMS and FDA evidence expectations in advance, the RAPID coverage pathway is designed to significantly reduce the review times that have historically occurred between FDA market authorization and Medicare national coverage determinations (NCDs). For devices completing the RAPID coverage pathway, a proposed NCD will be issued the same day as FDA market authorization, meaning that national Medicare coverage could begin as soon as 60 days after FDA market authorization. The public will have 60 days to comment on the procedural notice. CMS will respond to public comments in a subsequent final notice. Background Stakeholders have long sought a better way to cover new, innovative technologies. Today’s announcement is a critical step toward fulfilling the Trump administration’s commitment to provide accelerated and more predictable Medicare coverage for Breakthrough technologies that clinically benefit the Medicare population. RAPID Coverage Pathway at a Glance Download the RAPID Coverage Pathway Infographic (PDF) Device Eligibility Only devices that meet the following requirements are eligible for RAPID : Presumptive Class II FDA Breakthrough-designated devices participating in TAP planning to submit a De Novo request to FDA; 1 or Class III FDA Breakthrough-designated devices planning to submit a premarket approval application (PMA) regardless of whether they are participating in TAP; Devices in the IDE pre-submission stage, and the manufacturer plans to conduct an IDE study that enrolls Medicare beneficiaries and evaluates clinical outcomes that FDA determines are appropriate for the device and that CMS confirms evidence showing that the device achieves those outcomes in the Medicare beneficiary population would demonstrate that the device improves health outcomes for Medicare beneficiaries; Based on the information available, there is no evidence that immediately makes clear that the device will not fall under a Medicare benefit category; Not already the subject of a controlling Medicare NCD; Separately payable devices that can, if approved, be billed to Medicare; and Not otherwise excluded from coverage through law or regulation. FDA’s statutory definition of “device” includes in vitro diagnostic (IVD) products, such as diagnostic laboratory tests. IVDs, including diagnostic laboratory tests, are a highly specific area of coverage policy development, and CMS has historically delegated the review of many of these products to specialized Medicare Administrative Contractors (MACs). CMS believes that the majority of coverage determinations for IVDs granted Breakthrough Device designation should continue to be determined by the MACs through existing pathways. Therefore, IVD products will not be accepted into RAPID. Devices beyond the IDE pre-submission stage (such as those market authorized or with an IDE study underway) are not appropriate for RAPID. Under RAPID, CMS and FDA will leverage their early involvement in IDE pre-submission during the premarket phase. CMS National Coverage Determination Analysis and Timing After completing the IDE study, a manufacturer of a device in the RAPID coverage pathway will follow several steps to get national Medicare coverage, including submitting an NCD request letter and receiving FDA market authorization. If the device has demonstrated improved health outcomes, then CMS will initiate the NCD process by posting a tracking sheet and proposed NCD on the same day as FDA market authorization. There will be a 30-day public comment period on the proposed NCD. CMS’ goal is to release the final NCD approximately 60 days after FDA market authorization for Class II devices and 90 days for Class III devices. Evidence Development for RAPID National Coverage Determinations The improvement in clinical outcomes demonstrated in the IDE study and the device’s relative risk will determine if further evidence development (that is, coverage with evidence development [CED]) will be part of the NCD. At the time of FDA market authorization, lower risk devices are more likely to show that they are reasonable and necessary under 1862(a)(1)(A) of the Social Security Act (the Act), whereas higher risk devices are more likely to have remaining evidence gaps, necessitating additional evidence generation to qualify for coverage under 1862(a)(1)(A). If CMS believes a CED may be needed, CMS will engage with FDA and manufacturers before FDA market authorization to align potential CED requirements with any FDA-required post-approval studies. Duration of Coverage Under the RAPID Coverage Pathway RAPID NCDs will remain in effect until they are reconsidered. For RAPID NCDs issued under the CED framework, the notice emphasizes that CED NCDs are not meant to last indefinitely and that coverage under CED should be time-limited to facilitate the timely generation of sufficient evidence to inform patient and clinician decision making and to support a Medicare coverage determination under section 1862(a)(1)(A) of the Act. For more information on the RAPID coverage pathway, please visit: https://www.federalregister.gov/public-inspection/current ### ^ Includes 510(k) cleared devices where the primary predicate was authorized via the De Novo classification pathway no earlier than 18 months prior to acceptance into RAPID. title: Regulatory Alignment for Predictable and Immediate Device Coverage Pathway (CMS-3487-NC) Procedural Notice Inviting Comment

summary:
Objective

To evaluate the effects of intravenous iron on red cell transfusion and recovery after cardiac surgery.

Design

International, multicentre, double blind, placebo controlled randomised trial (ITACS).

Setting

33 hospitals across 10 countries. Participants were enrolled between July 2016 and December 2023.

Participants

955 adults with anaemia undergoing elective cardiac surgery. Exclusion criteria included haemoglobinopathy or iron storage disorder, renal dialysis, and erythropoietin or intravenous iron given in the previous four weeks.

Intervention

A computer generated program randomised participants to intravenous iron 1000 mg or placebo 1-26 weeks before surgery. Participants, clinicians, and data collectors were masked to the intervention.

Main outcome measures

The number of days alive and at home up to 90 days after surgery (primary outcome), red cell transfusion requirements and complications (secondary outcomes).

Results

Of 2993 screened participants, 955 were enrolled and 921 of the eligible 939 modified intention-to-treat participants were assessed for the primary outcome. The median number of days alive and at home up to 90 days after surgery was 81.1 (interquartile range 74.8-83.7) in patients assigned to intravenous iron and 80.0 (69.5-83.6) in those receiving placebo (adjusted median difference 1.0 day, 95.4% confidence interval 0.0 to 2.1 days, P=0.041). Red cell transfusions were given to 262 patients (61.1%) in the iron group and 302 (68.2%) in the placebo group during their hospital stay (relative risk 0.90, 95% confidence interval 0.82 to 0.99, P=0.027). No differences were observed for major complications or length of hospital stay.

Conclusion

Among patients with anaemia undergoing elective cardiac surgery, preoperative intravenous iron was associated with a reduction in red cell transfusion and a small improvement in the number of days alive and at home in the first 90 days after surgery. Intravenous iron is an effective component of patient blood management in this setting.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02632760.
title: Intravenous iron to treat anaemia before cardiac surgery (ITACS): international, double blind, placebo controlled randomised trial.

summary:
Objective

To assess the association between hospital accreditation inspections, which have historically included systematic evaluations of inpatient pain management practices, and opioid prescribing at hospital discharge.

Design

Quasi-experimental analysis.

Setting

US hospitals, stratified by hospital teaching status.

Participants

233 744 hospital admissions for Medicare beneficiaries with no Part D claim for opioids in the 90 days before hospital admission who were admitted near the dates of Joint Commission hospital accreditation visits.

Main outcome measure

The primary outcome was opioid prescribing to Medicare beneficiaries with no opioid claim in the 90 days before hospital admission during accreditation visits, leveraging the clinically arbitrary timing of these inspections for quasi-experimental analysis. Weekly per beneficiary rates of opioid prescription at discharge were compared with rates in the ±3 weeks surrounding the inspection to assess whether opioid prescribing at discharge increased during inspection weeks, when inpatient pain management practices are scrutinised.

Results

Overall, 21 156 hospital admissions at 90 teaching hospitals and 212 588 at 2400 non-teaching hospitals during 2008-18 were analysed. Patient characteristics were similar between inspection and surrounding non-inspection weeks for both hospital types. The adjusted odds of post-discharge opioid prescription was, however, 19% higher during inspection versus non-inspection weeks at teaching hospitals (1.19, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.05 to 1.34, P=0.007). Non-teaching hospitals showed no statistically significant change in opioid prescribing during inspection versus non-inspection weeks (adjusted odds ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.07, P=0.36).

Conclusion

Opioid prescribing at hospital discharge was higher among Medicare beneficiaries admitted to teaching hospitals during weeks of unannounced Joint Commission inspections compared with surrounding non-inspection weeks, raising the possibility that heightened focus on pain management may influence clinicians' decisions to prescribe opioids.
title: Opioid prescribing after Joint Commission hospital accreditation inspections: quasi-experimental analysis.

summary:
Objective

To determine whether an elevated head position (30-40°) improves functional outcomes compared with a flat head position (0-10°) in patients with acute ischaemic stroke caused by anterior circulation large vessel occlusion who have achieved successful reperfusion after endovascular thrombectomy.

Design

Multicentre, prospective, randomised, open label, blinded endpoint clinical trial.

Setting

67 comprehensive stroke centres in China, between 16 November 2023 and 23 January 2025.

Participants

1368 adults (aged ≥18 years) with acute ischaemic stroke caused by anterior circulation large vessel occlusion who achieved successful endovascular reperfusion, defined as an expanded thrombolysis in cerebral infarction score ≥2b after endovascular thrombectomy.

Interventions

Participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to maintain either an elevated head position (30-40°, n=685) or a flat head position (0-10°, n=683) for 72 hours after endovascular thrombectomy. MAIN: outcome measures The primary outcome was functional status at 90 days after randomisation, assessed by shift analysis of scores on the modified Rankin scale (range 0-6). The primary safety outcome was all cause mortality at 90 days after randomisation. Efficacy analyses used the randomised, full analysis set, and safety analyses used the safety population (identical to the randomised population). Adjusted models included age, baseline National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score (NIHSS), baseline Alberta Stroke Programme Early Computed Tomography Score, occlusion site, and time from last known well (ie, the last time when the patient was known to be at their usual neurological baseline before the current stroke event) to randomisation.

Results

In the population of 1368 randomised patients, the median age was 68 years, 565 participants (41.3%) were women, and 1358 (99.3%) completed the 90 day follow-up. The median baseline NIHSS score was 15, the median 90 day modified Rankin scale score was 3 (interquartile range (IQR) 1-5) in the head elevation group versus 3 (IQR 1-5) in the flat head position group (adjusted generalised odds ratio for a lower level of disability 1.12, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.97 to 1.29, P=0.14). All cause mortality at 90 days occurred in 125 (18.3%) of 682 patients in the elevated head position group and 137 (20.3%) of 676 patients in the flat head position group (adjusted risk ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.07, P=0.18).

Conclusions

72 hours of head elevation did not significantly improve 90 day functional outcomes versus flat head positioning in patients who had acute ischaemic stroke from large vessel occlusion with successful reperfusion after thrombectomy. The smaller than expected difference in results between the two groups leaves open the possibility of a modest but clinically meaningful benefit of head elevation in these patients.

Trial

registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06115707.
title: Head positioning after endovascular therapy for acute stroke due to large vessel occlusion (HeadSOAR): multicentre randomised controlled trial.

summary: Hyperkalaemia is a common and potentially life threatening electrolyte abnormality because of its association with malignant cardiac arrhythmias and sudden cardiac arrest. This condition is frequently encountered across acute and chronic care settings and disproportionately affects patients with comorbid conditions like chronic kidney disease, heart failure, diabetes mellitus, and those receiving drugs that impair renal potassium excretion. The most frequent causes of hyperkalaemia include impaired renal potassium elimination, from chronic kidney disease or pharmacological inhibition of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and transcellular potassium shifts resulting from metabolic acidosis, tissue breakdown, insulin deficiency, or hypertonic states. Despite its prevalence and clinical importance, substantial variability exists in the approach to diagnosis and management of hyperkalaemia, reflecting differences in definitions, risk stratification, and therapeutic approaches across clinical settings. Management strategies have evolved in recent years with improved understanding of potassium physiology and the availability of newer potassium binding agents, necessitating an updated synthesis of the evidence. In this state of the art review, we summarise contemporary data on the epidemiology and pathophysiology of hyperkalaemia, identify key risk factors and diagnostic considerations, and review evidence based approaches to acute and chronic management, with particular attention to special populations and high risk clinical scenarios.
title: Diagnosis and management of acute hyperkalaemia.

summary:
Objectives

To determine the range of possible prevalences of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) at death among National Football League (NFL) players and examine the association between CTE severity and risk of dementia.

Design

Retrospective population based cohort study.

Setting

NFL players from the era of hard-shell helmets (post-1949) in the US, including brain donors to the UNITE (Understanding Neurologic Injury and Traumatic Encephalopathy) and UCSF ADRC (University of California, San Francisco Alzheimer's Disease Research Center) brain banks.

Participants

1712 former NFL players who died during 2008-21, of whom 338 donated their brains for neuropathological evaluation. Personal information and causes of death according to the National Death Index (NDI) were obtained for all NFL players who died during the study period. Neuropathologists masked to clinical and playing histories assessed postmortem CTE diagnosis and stage IV CTE. Clinicians, masked to neuropathological status, reviewed donors' medical records and informant based clinical histories, to adjudicate a dementia diagnosis.

Main outcome measures

The main outcome measures were the minimum (number of donors with CTE/total number of NFL deaths) and maximum (1-(number of donors without CTE/total number of NFL deaths)) CTE prevalence at death during the study period and the six years (2016-21) when brain donation was most frequent. To account for selection pressure of brain donation status, inverse probability weighting was used to estimate the association between stage IV CTE and study clinician diagnosed dementia.

Results

Among 1712 NFL players who died, 338 (19.7%) players' brains were studied, 315 (93.2%) of whom had a diagnosis of CTE; thus, among all 1712 NFL players who died, the possible CTE prevalence at death ranged between 18.5% and 98.7%. The possible prevalence at death during 2016 to 2021, when brain donation was most frequent, ranged between 24.5% and 97.7%. Among brain donors, 104 (30.8%) had stage IV CTE, 202 (59.8%) had study clinician diagnosed dementia (dementia onset: 63.4 years, standard deviation (SD) 12.5; death: 73.1 years, SD 10.5), and 63 (18.6%) had neurodegenerative disease listed as primary cause of death. In donors, stage IV CTE was associated with study clinician diagnosed dementia (risk ratio 1.44, 95% confidence interval 1.16 to 1.78; P<0.001). Only 40.6% of donors (n=82) with study clinician diagnosed dementia had neurodegenerative disease listed as the primary or secondary cause of death.

Conclusions

At minimum, nearly a quarter of all former NFL players who died during 2016-21 had CTE neuropathology at death. Among NFL player brain donors, dementia diagnosed based on records before death was common and associated with stage IV CTE.
title: Prevalence of chronic traumatic encephalopathy at death in National Football League players: retrospective population based cohort study, 2008-21.

summary: Schizophrenia is a common and severe mental condition with onset usually in late adolescence and young adulthood. Schizophrenia is caused by a combination of multiple genetic and environmental factors with significant neurodevelopmental implications. Advances in the clinical management of schizophrenia include biological and non-biological treatments. Drug interventions can ameliorate positive symptoms and prevent the progression of disease due to relapses. Non-biological approaches such as psychosocial and cognitive interventions can help functional improvement, relapse prevention, and early stage psychosis management, and new interventions such as neuromodulation and digital health interventions are still under investigation. Despite these advances, novel therapeutic strategies, particularly drugs, are hampered by a biologically heterogeneous population of patients with schizophrenia, a condition defined only by clinical operational criteria. Reconsidering the construct of schizophrenia from the viewpoint of mechanism driven precision medicine will be important, with stratification of patients on the basis of their biological characteristics. The first step towards this goal is to accumulate objective biomarkers for schizophrenia. On the basis of the framework of precision medicine, further advancement in the management of schizophrenia is expected.
title: Schizophrenia: advances in pathophysiology, management, and precision medicine.

summary:
Background

Maternal folic acid prevents neural tube defects, but associations of parental folate and vitamin B12 with birth defects remain unclear.

Objective

To quantify associations of parental vitamin B12 and red blood cell (RBC) folate with offspring birth defects.

Design

Prospective cohort study.

Setting

Shanghai Preconception Cohort, China.

Participants

3032 couples (73 birth defect cases) with biomarkers sampled within 4 months before conception, and 17 765 women (327 birth defect cases) sampled at 4 months' gestation or earlier.

Measurements

Standardized predicted prevalences of birth defects ascertained among live births, stillbirths, and abortions due to fetal abnormalities were estimated using weighted logistic regression.

Results

Higher preconception parental levels of vitamin B12 were associated with lower predicted prevalences of birth defects in dose-response analyses. For preconception maternal vitamin B12 from the lowest (<148 pmol/L) to highest (≥590 pmol/L) categories, predicted prevalence decreased from 49.6 to 16.2 cases per 1000 pregnancies; paternal vitamin B12 showed a similar but attenuated pattern (55.5 to 24.0 cases per 1000 pregnancies). Preconception parental RBC folate showed imprecise patterns of lower predicted prevalence. For postconception maternal RBC folate, predicted prevalence was lower at levels of 906 to 1131 nmol/L than at levels below 453 nmol/L (16.5 vs. 25.7 cases per 1000 pregnancies), with little further reduction at higher levels. For postconception maternal vitamin B12, predicted prevalence changed little across lower categories but was lower at higher levels (11.8 vs. 20.4 cases per 1000 pregnancies at ≥590 vs. 148 to 294 pmol/L, respectively).

Limitation

Residual confounding.

Conclusion

Periconception parental vitamin B12 and postconception maternal RBC folate were associated with lower predicted prevalences of birth defects.

Primary funding source

National Key Research and Development Program of China, National Natural Science Foundation of China, and Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences.
title: Periconception Parental Red Blood Cell Folate, Vitamin B<sub>12</sub>, and Birth Defects in Offspring : A Prospective Cohort Study.

summary:
Objective

To assess the number, timing, characteristics, and scholarly impact of secondary publications generated using individual participant level data (IPD) from a portfolio of clinical trials shared with external investigators through a data sharing platform.

Design

Cross sectional study.

Setting

Yale University Open Data Access (YODA) Project platform.

Participants

Johnson & Johnson sponsored clinical trials listed on the YODA Project platform with IPD available for external sharing through 2021 and with a full length, peer reviewed publication (that is, primary publication) reporting primary endpoint results by the original trial investigators.

Main outcome measures

Number, timing, research objectives, analysis type, and scholarly impact of secondary publications using IPD from these trials identified through Web of Science citation searches of primary publications through June 2025. Scholarly impact metrics included journal impact factor, annual citation count, and annual Altmetric Attention Score. Secondary publications were classified as internal (authored by at least one original trial investigator) or external.

Results

Among 336 eligible trials, 265 (79%) had at least one associated secondary publication, totalling 1167 publications, of which 209 (17.9%) were external. Among external publications with a reported data access mechanism (n=190; 91%), most obtained access through data sharing platforms (n=161; 85%), primarily the YODA Project (n=157; 83%). Over time, the proportion of external publications increased steadily, exceeding 50% of all secondary publications by year 11 and thereafter. Compared with internal publications, external publications were more frequently pooled analyses (151/209 (72%) v 534/958 (55.7%); P<0.001) and involved predictive or prognostic modelling (108/209 (51.7%) v 322/958 (33.6%); P<0.001), development of statistical models or algorithms (60/209 (29%) v 114/958 (11.9%); P<0.001), and validation of existing methods, models, or risk scores (32/209 (15%) v 66/958 (6.9%); P<0.001). Compared with internal publications, external publications were published in journals with higher impact factors (median 6.7 (interquartile range 3.4-16.6) v 4.6 (2.9-10.2); P=0.002) and had higher annual Altmetric Attention Scores (median 2.1 (0.7-7.1) v 0.6 (0.3-2.3); P<0.001) but had lower annual citation counts (median 2.7 (1.1-5.6) v 3.4 (1.6-7.5); P<0.001) and were less likely to be cited in clinical guidelines (21/184 (11%) v 235/805 (29.2%); P<0.001) or policy documents (14/184 (8%) v 206/805 (25.6%); P<0.001).

Conclusions

Most trials in this portfolio of clinical trials, for which IPD were available through a data sharing platform, generated secondary research by both original trial investigators and external investigators. External investigators most often accessed data through the data sharing platform, and their publications accounted for an increasingly larger proportion of secondary publications over time. These findings suggest that structured data sharing mechanisms may support additional secondary use of clinical trial data and further enhance the scientific value of clinical trials.
title: Secondary use and scholarly impact of a portfolio of clinical trials with shared individual participant level data: cross sectional study.

summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved Zanvastro (zilganersen) injection for the treatment of Alexander disease in pediatric and adult patients. Zanvastro is the first FDA-approved treatment for Alexander disease and the first therapy to directly target the protein buildup that drives the disease. “For patients with Alexander disease and their families, there have been no approved treatment options — only supportive care while the disease progresses,” said Emily Freilich, M.D., Director of the Division of Neurology I in the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. “Today’s approval is a landmark moment for this community, offering the first therapy that addresses the underlying cause of this rare and serious disease.” Alexander disease is a rare, progressive neurological disorder caused by mutations in the gene that produces glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). When this protein is abnormal, it accumulates in the brain’s supportive cells, causing damage to the nervous system over time. The disease affects less than 1 in a million people and can cause a wide range of serious and potentially life-threatening problems, including seizures, loss of developmental milestones, difficulty walking, muscle weakness, and increased pressure in the brain. Zanvastro is an antisense oligonucleotide — a type of medicine that works by reducing the production of the abnormal GFAP protein before it can accumulate and cause further damage. It is administered as an injection into the spinal canal every three months by a trained healthcare professional. The efficacy and safety of Zanvastro were evaluated in a multicenter, randomized, controlled clinical study (NCT04849741) enrolling 49 pediatric and adult patients with Alexander disease 2 years of age and older, and in an open-label substudy of 4 patients less than 2 years of age. Because Alexander disease is so rare and can affect patients across a wide range of ages, the FDA evaluated the available evidence in support of an indication covering patients from infancy through adulthood. In patients aged 5 years and older who had measurable difficulties with walking at baseline, those treated with Zanvastro showed significantly better walking speed at 61 weeks compared to those who received no treatment. In children aged 2 to 4 years, where walking speed is not a reliable measure of progress, a broader assessment of motor skills — including standing, walking, running, and jumping — was used instead. Children treated with Zanvastro showed improvement on this measure while those in the control group declined. For patients under 2 years of age, direct clinical trial data were limited by the rarity of the disease and lack of concurrent control. Pharmacokinetic modeling confirmed that drug levels in this age group are expected to be similar to those seen in older children at the same dose. This observation was also supported by safety data from four patients under 2 years of age treated in the study, as well as the safety data observed in the older pediatric patients. This approach supported extending the indication to the youngest patients while maintaining the evidentiary standards required to support approval. The most common side effects of Zanvastro are vomiting, back pain, cough, headache, and post-lumbar puncture syndrome. Patients and caregivers should inform their healthcare provider if symptoms consistent with meningitis develop, as aseptic meningitis has been reported in patients treated with Zanvastro. Patients and providers should carefully review the full prescribing information when making treatment decisions. Zanvastro received Orphan Drug, Fast Track, Breakthrough Therapy, and Rare Pediatric Disease and Priority Review Voucher designations, reflecting the serious and rare nature of Alexander disease, and FDA’s commitment to rare disease drug development. The approval of Zanvastro for the treatment of Alexander disease was granted to Ionis Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
