summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) translate research evidence into actionable recommendations, but their development faces mounting challenges. With dozens of trials and systematic reviews published daily, the traditional 18- to 24-month development cycle struggles to incorporate emerging evidence, and manual screening, synthesis, and quality assessment consume thousands of person-hours per guideline. The resulting knowledge translation pipeline is slow, inconsistent, and quickly outdated. <strong>Objective:</strong> This review aimed to chart the computational methods empirically tested for automating CPG development, the tasks they address, and their evaluation measures, and to map where that evidence is concentrated and where it is absent for living guidelines. <strong>Methods:</strong> The review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute scoping review framework and PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidance. We searched PubMed and Scopus for studies published between January 2001 and December 2025, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching. Eligible studies used automated methods for a guideline development task, reported original research with empirical testing, and gave sufficient methodological detail. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data. Findings were charted across 4 pillars: retrieval, extraction, encoding, and evaluation. <strong>Results:</strong> A total of 47 studies met eligibility criteria, spanning 2001 to 2025, with a marked increase after 2015 and a surge in large language model (LLM) work in 2024-2025. Pillar counts (nonexclusive) were as follows: retrieval, 6; extraction, 15; encoding, 26; and evaluation, 17. In retrieval pillar, query expansion achieved 80% recall, while semantic search tools traded recall for specificity (98%). In extraction, rule-based natural language processing achieved an F-measure of 81.96% for structured clinical actions and 71.75% for patient states, and hybrid ontology methods covered 86% of eligibility criteria; LLMs performed well on structured fields but degraded on interpretive content. In encoding, approaches progressed from formalisms such as Guideline Interchange Format version 3 (GLIF3) and guideline elements model toward Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR)–based representation; semiautomated tools assisted guideline encoding, and logic verification detected inconsistencies and coverage gaps missed by human reviewers. In evaluation, LLM appraisers assigned higher Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation II (AGREE II) scores than human appraisers, by a mean difference of 12.5% in one study (95% limits of agreement –30.6% to 55.5%; intraclass correlation coefficient 0.753) and by 22 to 60 percentage points across domains in another. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Automation shows promise for bounded, well-structured guideline development tasks, while robust evidence for end-to-end, production-scale living guideline pipelines remains limited. No included study demonstrated a validated pipeline connecting all 4 pillars in an operating guideline program, and evidence on clinical safety, workflow integration, and cost-effectiveness is largely absent. Realizing living guidelines will require interoperability standards such as FHIR, and evaluation in real guideline production rather than retrospective benchmarks.
title: Automation of Living Clinical Practice Guideline Development: Scoping Review

summary: Calendar Year (CY) 2027 End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) Prospective Payment System Final Rule — CMS-1846-F Combating kidney disease starts with prevention, early detection, and timely treatment to help protect kidney health and slow disease progression. For Americans who depend on dialysis, high-quality care is vital to their health and daily lives. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) is committed to improving how our kidney care system serves patients by supporting access to lifesaving treatment so more Americans can live longer, healthier lives. CMS is advancing its goals for dialysis access and quality through the calendar year (CY) 2027 Medicare End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) Prospective Payment System (PPS) final rule. On Oct. 28, 2026, CMS issued a final rule to update payment rates and policies under the ESRD PPS for renal dialysis services furnished to Medicare beneficiaries on or after Jan. 1, 2027. This rule also finalizes updates to the acute kidney injury (AKI) dialysis payment rate for renal dialysis services furnished by ESRD facilities for calendar year (CY) 2027 and updates requirements for the ESRD Quality Incentive Program (QIP). For CY 2027, CMS will increase the ESRD PPS base rate to $297.52, which CMS expects will increase total payments to all ESRD facilities, both freestanding and hospital-based, by approximately 2.7%. This amount includes a $12.85 increase to account for the incorporation of phosphate binders into the ESRD PPS base rate. The CY 2027 ESRD PPS final rule also finalizes changes to the low-volume payment adjustment, changes to the payment adjustments for pediatric patients, an increase to the home and self-dialysis training add-on payment adjustment amount, and modifications to the transitional drug add-on payment adjustment (TDAPA), and modifications to the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment policies. Beginning with Payment Year (PY) 2029, CMS is replacing the Hypercalcemia reporting measure with the Facility-Level Percentage of Chronic Hyperphosphatemia in Dialysis Patients (Hyperphosphatemia) clinical measure and removing two reporting measures from the ESRD QIP. CMS is also updating the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) Bloodstream Infection (BSI) in Hemodialysis Patients clinical measure national baseline data and risk-adjustment methodology. Additionally, CMS is updating the measure domains and the domain and measure weights used to calculate the total performance score. CMS also summarizes input received on a request for information on the potential inclusion of the Dialysis Facility Discussion of Patient Life Goals (D-PaLS) Patient-Reported Outcome Performance measure (PRO-PM) in the ESRD QIP. Final Updates to the ESRD PPS for CY 2027 The ESRD PPS provides a bundled, per-treatment payment to ESRD facilities that includes all renal dialysis services furnished for outpatient maintenance dialysis, including drugs and biological products. Additionally, the bundled payment includes all other renal dialysis items and services that were formerly separately payable under previous payment methodologies. The bundled payment rate is case-mix adjusted for several factors relating to patient characteristics. There are also facility-level adjustments for low patient volume, for ESRD facilities in rural areas, and for ESRD facilities in certain noncontiguous states and territories, as well as a wage index adjustment. When applicable, the bundled payment rate also includes a training payment for home and self-dialysis modalities; an outlier payment for high-cost patients; add-on payment adjustments for certain drugs, equipment, and supplies; and a pediatric ESRD add-on payment adjustment (through 2026). Annual Update to the ESRD PPS Base Rate Under the ESRD PPS for CY 2027, Medicare expects to pay $7.0 billion to approximately 7,600 ESRD facilities for furnishing renal dialysis services. The final CY 2027 ESRD PPS base rate is $297.52, which is an increase of $15.81 from the current CY 2026 base rate of $281.71. This amount includes $12.85 to reflect the inclusion of phosphate binders into the ESRD PPS base rate. Additionally, this amount reflects the application of the final wage index budget neutrality adjustment factor (1.00260), the final CY 2027 ESRD Bundled market basket update of 1.9%, and a budget neutrality factor of 0.98864 for the budget neutral changes to low-volume, pediatric, and home and self-dialysis training payment adjustments, equaling $297.52 [ ($281.71 + $12.85) x 1.00260 x 0.98864) x 1.019 = $297.52]. CMS projects that the CY 2027 updates will increase the total payments to all ESRD facilities by 2.7% compared with CY 2026. Hospital-based and freestanding ESRD facilities are both projected to have an estimated 2.7% increase in total payments. Wage Index Update CMS is making routine annual updates to the ESRD PPS-specific wage index that is used to adjust ESRD PPS payments for geographic differences in area wages. The ESRD PPS wage index methodology, finalized in the CY 2025 ESRD PPS final rule, combines data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Occupational Employment & Wage Statistics (OEWS) program and freestanding ESRD facility cost reports to produce the ESRD PPS-specific wage index. We are updating the ESRD PPS wage index for CY 2027 to use the latest available BLS OEWS data. CMS will continue to apply the wage-index floor of 0.6000 and a 5 % cap on wage-index decreases from the prior year, as finalized in the CY 2023 ESRD PPS final rule. Updates to the Outlier Policy CMS is making routine updates to the fixed dollar loss (FDL) and Medicare allowable payment (MAP) amounts for CY 2027. For pediatric beneficiaries, the final FDL amount will increase from $162.43 to $229.49, and the final MAP amount will increase from $50.19 to $63.27 as compared to CY 2026 values. For adult beneficiaries, the final FDL amount will increase from $14.80 to $90.60, and the final MAP amount will increase from $23.68 to $41.83. These increases are primarily attributable to the projected utilization of new drugs that will be ESRD outlier services in CY 2027. Addition to the ESRD PPS Base Rate for the Inclusion of Phosphate Binders CMS is finalizing its proposal to permanently increase the ESRD PPS base rate to account for the costs of phosphate binders, marking the completion of the incorporation of phosphate binders into the bundled payment, which began Jan. 1, 2025. This additional amount of $12.85 is based on the most recent average sales price (ASP) data for each of the six types of phosphate binders and on utilization during the TDAPA period, and includes operational costs equal to 6% of ASP. Low-Volume Payment Adjustment CMS is finalizing its proposal to increase the Low-Volume Payment Adjustment (LVPA) volume threshold from 4,000 to 8,000 treatments. This change will also expand the number of LVPA tiers from two to six. ESRD facilities with fewer than 3,000 median treatments over the past three cost reporting years will receive the greatest payment adjuster and ESRD facilities with between 7,000 and 7,999 median treatments will receive the smallest adjuster. We are also finalizing an extension to the attestation deadline for payment year 2027. ESRD facilities may attest that they meet the requirements of the LVPA up to Dec. 31, 2026, to receive the LVPA for CY 2027. This budget-neutral change will reduce the ESRD PPS base rate by approximately 1.1% (~$3). The updated LVPA adjustment will better align payments with costs by recognizing that ESRD facilities furnishing between 4,000 and 8,000 treatments annually generally incur higher costs than higher-volume facilities. Payment Adjustments for Pediatric Patients CMS is finalizing its proposal to modify the payment adjustments for renal dialysis services furnished to pediatric ESRD patients to align with the end of the temporary pediatric payment adjustment in 2027. We are finalizing two permanent changes that will appropriately recognize the higher costs for ESRD facilities that treat pediatric patients. First, we are updating the case-mix adjusters for pediatric patients based on more recent cost data. This addresses the inherent higher costs for patients under 18 years of age. Second, we are finalizing our proposal to begin applying the LVPA to treatments furnished to pediatric ESRD beneficiaries by ESRD facilities that meet the low-volume criteria. Data analysis shows that smaller facilities incur high costs even in the pediatric ESRD patient population. These two changes will result in roughly the same expected spending on pediatric patients, but with payments better targeted toward lower-volume ESRD facilities with higher anticipated resource use and younger pediatric ESRD patients. We are finalizing these changes on a budget-neutral basis. Home and Self-Dialysis Training Add-on Payment Adjustment CMS is finalizing an increase to the payment adjustment amount for home and self-dialysis training from $95.60 to $138.00 beginning in CY 2027. We are also finalizing our proposal to allow the add-on payment adjustment for home and self-dialysis training during the onset period (the first four months of ESRD dialysis), during which the ESRD PPS does not currently pay the home and self-dialysis training add-on adjustment. We are finalizing a reduction to the onset adjustment factor to account for payment overlap during the onset period. The CY 2027 onset adjustment factor is 1.311. These changes will better align the training payment with the actual cost of training patients and caretakers to perform home and self-dialysis. We are finalizing these changes on a budget-neutral basis. Changes to the TDAPA and Post-TDAPA Add-on Payment Adjustment Policies CMS is finalizing several changes to better align payment adjustment amounts for the TDAPA and post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment with the actual costs of drugs. CMS is finalizing its proposal to use older ASP data when current ASP data are unavailable, such as when the reported ASP reflects zero or negative sales. However, when a drug manufacturer fails to report ASP data to CMS, payment under the TDAPA or Post-TDAPA Add-on Payment Adjustment would be discontinued in accordance with our longstanding conditional ASP policy. CMS is also finalizing a proposal to update the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment quarterly through change requests throughout the year, ensuring that the post-TDAPA add-on payment adjustment is based on the most recent pricing and utilization data available. Changes to the Payment for Renal Dialysis Services Furnished to Individuals with AKI As required by section 1834(r) of the Social Security Act, CMS is updating the AKI dialysis payment rate for CY 2027 to $297.52, which is equal to the final CY 2027 ESRD PPS base rate. CMS uses the CY 2027 ESRD PPS wage index to calculate AKI dialysis payments. The increase to the home and self-dialysis training payment adjustment amount under the ESRD PPS will apply to training payments for AKI dialysis. Starting in CY 2027, ESRD facilities are responsible for providing medically necessary phosphate binders to beneficiaries with AKI that are under their direct care. Final Updates to the ESRD QIP The ESRD QIP is authorized by law, and under the program, CMS assesses the total performance of each facility on quality measures specified for a payment year, applies an appropriate payment reduction to each facility that does not meet a minimum total performance score (mTPS), and publicly reports the results. CMS is removing the Hypercalcemia reporting measure and replacing it with the Hyperphosphatemia clinical measure beginning with PY 2029. The Hyperphosphatemia clinical measure will help drive decreases in cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, and overall mortality by incentivizing additional interventions such as nutritional counseling, phosphorus binding medications, or adjustment of dialysis prescription. summary: Background: Frailty is prevalent among hospitalized patients and is associated with increased risk of complications, prolonged hospitalization, higher mortality, and health care costs. Existing frailty screening tools, including the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) and Hospital Frailty Risk Score (HFRS), have limitations related to subjectivity, resource intensity, or reliance on retrospective data, limiting their use in routine acute care. Early identification of frailty is critical to support targeted interventions and resource allocation, yet scalable approaches for predicting frailty early during hospital admission remain limited. Objective: This paper evaluates whether routinely collected electronic medical record (EMR) data available within the first 72 hours of admission can be used to predict frailty in hospitalized patients. Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using routinely collected EMR data from the Royal Adelaide Hospital (RAH), including overnight admissions with a length of stay of at least 72 hours between July 2023 and December 2024. Frailty was defined using the HFRS (score >4). Predictors were derived from EMR data available within 72 hours of admission, including demographics, medications, laboratory results, nursing assessments, and medical and allied health consult orders. Data were split into training (21,436/26,824, 80%) and test (5388/26,824, 20%) sets. Multiple machine learning models were trained, with the -score as the primary optimization metric. Model performance was evaluated using the -score, recall, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), calibration, and clinical utility analyses. Results: This study included 26,824 admissions, of whom 9427 (35%) were classified as frail. The final XGBoost (XGB) model achieved an -score of 0.755 (95% CI 0.741-0.768), an AUROC of 0.777 (95% CI 0.764-0.790), and a recall of 0.873 (95% CI 0.857-0.887) on the test dataset, with good calibration and an expected-to-observed ratio close to 1 (0.996, 95% CI 0.963-1.028). Key predictors included polypharmacy, laboratory results (including creatinine, albumin, and sodium), allied health consult orders, and nursing assessment data. Model performance was lower at 24 hours postadmission and improved by discharge. Conclusions: An EMR-based frailty prediction model using data available at 72 hours postadmission can identify patients with frailty early in their hospital stay, supporting targeted interventions and operational planning. Reduced performance in Indigenous patients highlights the need for culturally validated frailty indices and ongoing evaluation of equity in predictive modeling.
title: Development and Internal Validation of an Electronic Medical Record–Based Machine Learning Model for Frailty Prediction in Hospitalized Patients: Retrospective Cohort Study

summary:
Objective

To test the efficacy and cost effectiveness of high volume injections with and without corticosteroid versus sham injection for midportion Achilles tendinopathy.

Design

Single centred, participant and assessor masked, three arm randomised controlled trial (Inject trial).

Setting

Community.

Participants

From 5 December 2019 and 24 July 2022, 192 adults (18 years or older) diagnosed with midportion Achilles tendinopathy were randomly assigned (1:1:1) to sham (n=64), high volume injection without corticosteroid (n=63), or high volume injection with corticosteroid (n=65).

Interventions

Participants were allocated to sham injection (2-3 mL 0.5% bupivacaine hydrochloride), high volume injection with corticosteroid (50 mL saline and 0.5% bupivacaine with 25 mg hydrocortisone in the first 10 mL), or high volume injection with no corticosteroid (same solution but without hydrocortisone). They received the same exercise programme, education, and activity modification advice.

Main outcome measures

The primary clinical outcome was pain and disability using the validated VISA-A and the primary endpoint was at 52 weeks. The economic outcome was cost per quality-adjusted life-years from a societal perspective.

Results

VISA-A data were obtained from 181 (94%) of 192 participants at 12 months. No clear differences were noted between sham and high volume injection either with (-3.5 (98.33% confidence interval -12.0 to 5.0)) or without corticosteroid (4.0 (-4.2 to 12.3)), and between the two injections (-7.5 (-15.3 to 0.3)), at 12 months. The point estimate was closest to the target difference for the comparison between injections and favoured the arm without steroid. The only differences observed on VISA-A at intermediate time points were a benefit for high volume with corticosteroid versus sham at six weeks (9.2 (1.5 to 16.9)) but worse outcomes for high volume injection with corticosteroid versus high volume injection with no corticosteroid at 26 weeks (-8.6 (-16.4 to -0.7)). The health economic analysis found high volume injection with corticosteroid to be less costly than the sham with similar effectiveness based on quality-adjusted life-years (>0.90 probability of being cost effective at $AUD50 000 and $100 000 willingness-to-pay thresholds). No serious trial related adverse events were recorded.

Conclusion

High volume injections with or without corticosteroids did not improve pain or disability compared with sham at 12 months. Although high volume injections with corticosteroid showed short term clinical benefit and potential reduction in healthcare costs over a year, they were associated with worse longer term clinical outcomes. The clinical data do not support routine use for high volume injections with corticosteroid for midportion Achilles tendinopathy.

Trial registration

Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry ACTRN12619001455156.
title: Efficacy and cost effectiveness of high volume injections with and without corticosteroid compared with sham for midportion Achilles tendinopathy (Inject trial): randomised controlled trial.

summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as conversational agents for communication and guidance, but their ability to adapt responses to a patient’s emotional state and literacy level remains insufficiently characterized. In patient-facing scenarios, effective communication requires not only accurate medical content but also appropriate tone, clarity, and responsiveness to user vulnerability. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate, within a controlled, single-scenario experimental design, the ability of contemporary LLMs to adapt medical guidance responses to different levels of emotional sensitivity and literacy, and to assess their consistency in both generating and interpreting such adaptations. Methods: A controlled benchmark was designed to evaluate how 4 LLMs adapt medical guidance responses to predefined emotional and literacy levels for a realistic patient profile asking an open-ended question. To establish a robust performance baseline, one model was deployed locally (Gemma 3 27B), and 3 are cloud-based (Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, and GPT 5.2). Each model was tested across all combinations of 5 emotional levels, 3 literacy levels, and 3 prompt-verbosity variants, yielding 45 responses per model. Generated responses were assessed against human-reviewed ground truth for emotional and literacy alignment. A separate self-evaluation procedure measured each model’s ability to interpret its own outputs using the same adaptation framework. The study also examined generation-interpretation consistency and quantitative text properties, with particular attention to response length and verbosity. Results: Literacy adaptation was consistently accurate across models, often achieving near-zero error, indicating strong capability in adjusting explanatory complexity. In contrast, emotional adaptation showed greater variability and was more sensitive to model architecture and prompt design. The larger cloud-based models demonstrated more stable performance overall, while the local model exhibited higher variability, particularly under shorter prompts. A systematic asymmetry was observed between generation and interpretation. The models frequently misclassified low emotional and literacy levels as “normal,” suggesting limitations in recognizing user needs. Quantitative analysis revealed that response length increased with both emotional sensitivity and literacy level, with prompt verbosity and model-specific tendencies acting as secondary factors. Conclusions: Within our scenario, current LLMs demonstrated the capacity to support adaptive medical guidance, but their performance was uneven across dimensions, especially in terms of emotional generation and interpretation. For health care applications, these systems should be treated as assistive tools under human oversight rather than as autonomous communicators, with careful consideration of ethical, privacy, and safety implications in sensitive health contexts. title: Emotional and Literacy Adaptation in Large Language Model–Based Medical Guidance: Development and Usability Study

summary: Background: Hypothyroidism is a prevalent endocrine disorder characterized by an insidious onset and nonspecific symptoms, often leading to significant diagnostic delays. While biochemical thyroid function tests (TFTs) are the gold standard, their invasive nature and cost make them impractical for continuous, proactive screening of at-risk populations. Thyroid hormones exert direct chronotropic effects on the cardiovascular system, and their levels are closely correlated with heart rate (HR). Wearable devices capable of continuous HR monitoring offer a novel opportunity for noninvasive, digital phenotype–based detection. Objective: This study aimed to develop and validate an AI-assisted system that uses wearable-derived sleep HR data as a digital monitoring tool for individuals at risk of hypothyroidism, helping identify those who warrant further confirmatory thyroid testing. Methods: This retrospective cohort study used 1677 paired observations consisting of sleep HR data and serum TFT results, including free thyroxine (T4) and thyroid-stimulating hormone levels, from 413 participants (mean age 43.1, SD 9.7 y; women: n=314, 76%). Participants wore consumer-grade wearables (Fitbit) that recorded HR and sleep data. Each TFT result was paired with sleep HR data extracted from the 15 consecutive nights preceding the blood test. An AI system was developed using a gradient boosting algorithm (LightGBM) to classify thyroid status by integrating baseline TFT results with statistical and temporal HR features. The model’s performance was evaluated using patient-level leave-one-out cross-validation. To examine the benefit of longitudinal data, performance was compared using 1, 2, or 3 prior paired observations as reference points. Results: To ensure clinical relevance and avoid performance inflation from hyperthyroid cases, we prioritized the analysis of a subset containing only euthyroid and hypothyroid data (n=744 paired observations). In this clinically challenging subset, the system achieved an accuracy of 74.6%, with a sensitivity of 82% and a specificity of 73.5% using a single-reference data pair. Incorporating longitudinal HR patterns further enhanced performance; using 3 reference pairs improved accuracy to 78.1% (sensitivity 81.8% and specificity 77.7%). In the overall dataset (n=1677 paired observations), the system demonstrated an accuracy of 80.8%, with a sensitivity of 82% and a specificity of 80.8% using a single-reference pair. Notably, the system achieved high clinical safety by detecting 96.3% of severe overt hypothyroidism cases (free T4 <0.5 ng/dL). Conclusions: This AI-assisted system demonstrates the feasibility of a sensitive, noninvasive longitudinal monitoring tool for hypothyroidism, robustly identifying a high proportion of hypothyroid cases—particularly severe ones—to prioritize at-risk individuals for confirmatory blood tests. Given the predominantly female iatrogenic-withdrawal cohort, prospective sex-balanced validation in primary hypothyroidism is warranted.
title: Harnessing AI for Hypothyroidism Monitoring Using Wearable-Derived Heart Rate Data: Retrospective Cohort Study

summary:
Objective

To describe the epidemiological characteristics, public health response, and evidence of international spread of a large measles outbreak that contributed to the loss of Canada's measles elimination status.

Design

Descriptive analysis of the cohort of measles outbreak cases reported to Ontario's public health surveillance system during the outbreak period: epidemiological week of 28 October 2024 to 6 October 2025.

Setting

Ontario, Canada.

Participants

Individuals meeting the outbreak case definition for confirmed or probable measles infection during the outbreak period.

Exposure

Exposure to measles virus associated with the Ontario outbreak and related transmission chains.

Main outcome measures

Demographic characteristics, vaccination status, admission to hospital, complications, pregnancy associated outcomes, mortality, and evidence of international spread based on measles virus genotyping and sequencing. Cases were identified using an outbreak-specific case definition incorporating epidemiological, clinical, laboratory, and viral sequencing criteria. Phylogenetic analysis of measles virus sequences was used to assess evidence of onwards spread to other countries.

Results

The outbreak consisted of 2377 cases (2064 confirmed and 313 probable) over 49 weeks and contributed to the loss of Canada's measles elimination status. Most cases (2146/2377, 90.3%) occurred among members of historically under-vaccinated communities, with limited spillover into the broader population. Among the 2377 cases, approximately three quarters of cases (n=1736, 73.0%) occurred in individuals aged 19 years or younger, 2121 (89.2%) were unvaccinated, and 97 (4.1%) had unknown vaccination status. The outbreak was associated with 166 (7%) admissions to hospital, 13 (<1%) admissions to intensive care unit, 51 (2.1%) infections during pregnancy, 10 (<1%) congenital measles infections, one (<1%) case of encephalitis, and one (<1%) infant death. Sequencing identified a novel N450 distinct sequence identifier that was subsequently detected in countries including the United States of America, Mexico, and the Netherlands. The outbreak strain was designated a World Health Organization named strain (MVs/Ontario.CAN/47.24).

Conclusions

These findings highlight the risk of measles re-establishment in countries that have attained elimination and underscore the importance of culturally appropriate community engagement to build trust in immunisation and prevent future outbreaks. This outbreak shows the fragility of measles elimination in the presence of long standing immunity gaps within interconnected communities across the Americas and the population-level protection that limited broader community transmission.
title: Impact of a large measles outbreak associated with transmission in the Americas and Canada's loss of measles elimination status: descriptive cohort study.

summary:
Importance

For patients with atrioventricular block requiring high-burden ventricular pacing, the optimal pacing strategy to reduce heart failure (HF) and all-cause mortality remains uncertain. Robust comparative evidence on the clinical outcomes of left bundle-branch area pacing (LBBAP) vs right ventricular pacing (RVP) in this population is needed.

Objective

To compare 24-month clinical outcomes of LBBAP vs RVP in patients with atrioventricular block and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF; ≥50%).

Design, setting, and participants

The LEAP-Block study was a prospective, multicenter, randomized, controlled, superiority trial conducted across 14 Chinese hospitals from January 2021 to August 2025, with last follow-up on June 3, 2025. Of 551 patients with LVEF 50% or greater requiring ventricular pacing who underwent eligibility assessment, 499 with anticipated ventricular pacing greater than 40% were randomized.

Interventions

Patients were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to LBBAP (n = 249) or RVP (n = 250).

Main outcomes and measures

The primary end point was a composite of all-cause death, HF events, or upgrade to biventricular pacing at 24 months. Secondary end points included pacing-induced cardiomyopathy and device-related complications.

Results

The primary analysis included 482 patients (LBBAP, n = 242; RVP, n = 240; mean age, 67 years; 46% female). Acute procedure success was comparable between the 2 groups (LBBAP, 237/242 [97.9%] vs RVP, 239/240 [99.6%]; P = .22), with left bundle-branch capture confirmed in 188 of 236 patients (79.7%). LBBAP significantly reduced the primary end point vs RVP (2.4% vs 12.5%, respectively; absolute risk difference, -10.1% [95% CI, -16.8% to -3.4%]; P = .003). Among secondary outcomes, the LBBAP group had fewer HF events (3.4% vs 11.3%; -7.9% [95% CI, -13.0% to -2.8%]). No significant differences were observed in all-cause death, biventricular pacing upgrade, device-related complications, or pacing-induced cardiomyopathy. The 24-month Kaplan-Meier estimated cumulative incidence of the primary end point was 5.0% for LBBAP vs 13.2% for RVP (hazard ratio, 0.37 [95% CI, 0.19 to 0.73]; P = .004). LBBAP superiority was consistent across all prespecified subgroups.

Conclusions and relevance

Among patients with atrioventricular block and preserved LVEF requiring high-burden ventricular pacing, LBBAP was superior to RVP in reducing the risk of the composite end point of all-cause death, HF events, or upgrade to biventricular pacing at 24 months.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04730921.
title: Left Bundle-Branch Area Pacing vs Right Ventricular Pacing for Atrioventricular Block and Preserved Left Ventricular Function: The LEAP-Block Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary: Background: The rapid rise of secure patient messaging has transformed ophthalmic communication, with text volumes now exceeding prepandemic levels across health care systems. Our study uses a natural language processing (NLP) model to explore patterns in over 30,000 secure messages and identify common ocular complaints and differences by patient demographics. Objective: The objective of this study is to characterize the clinical and administrative concerns communicated through secure ophthalmology messaging and to assess differences in message content across patient sociodemographic groups. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional study of deidentified, patient-initiated secure messages sent between June 2014 and July 2024. Patients with ophthalmic conditions who initiated secure electronic health record (EHR) portal messages were included. Of the 52,388 extracted message threads, 30,390 (58%) patient medical advice request (PMAR) messages routed solely to the Department of Ophthalmology from 4817 unique patients were assessed after the exclusion of questionnaires, courtesy messages, clinician responses, and messages routed to other health care departments. Of these unique patients, 2673 (55.5%) were female, 2740 (56.9%) were aged 50 years or older, 2346 (48.7%) were White, 4392 (91.2%) were non-Hispanic, and 2774 (57.6%) were married. NLP and large language model (LLM)–assisted topic classification were used to categorize message content. The distribution of message topics and frequency of clinical concerns were assessed and stratified by age, sex, race, ethnicity, and marital status. Differences in message frequency by demographic subgroup were assessed using 2-proportion z-tests. Results: Following preprocessing and topic modeling, 14,284 (47%) of the 30,390 messages could be predefined in relation to a topic cluster and were included in the final analysis. Nearly half of all 14,284 predefined messages addressed administrative issues, including 4166 (29.2%) scheduling-related inquiries, 1352 (9.5%) pharmacy and medication refill requests, and 581 (4.1%) insurance document issues. Among clinical concerns, of the total 14,284 predefined messages, 2975 (20.8%) messages involved vision disturbances, 1241 (8.7%) involved glaucoma-related symptoms, 1074 (7.5%) involved tumor-related questions, and 1064 (7.4%) involved surgery-relevant concerns. Message content differed significantly by demographic characteristics. Non-White patients more frequently raised issues related to pharmacy refills, insurance, glaucoma, and disability documentation, whereas White patients more often reported surgical concerns. Older patients more frequently messaged about glaucoma, surgery, and tumor-related issues, while female patients more often reported complications and swelling or infection. Conclusions: Secure patient messages frequently include clinically relevant symptoms with potential triage implications and demonstrate demographic differences in care-seeking behavior. Systematic analysis of message content may support safer triage, improved workflow efficiency, and more equitable delivery of ophthalmic care.
title: Secure Patient Messaging in Ophthalmology: Retrospective Natural Language Processing Study

summary: Meyer-Keirath and colleagues found no significant difference in posttreatment symptoms between video-based and face-to-face psychotherapy. However, the wide confidence interval indicates substantial imprecision, while the prediction interval suggests that comparative effects may vary considerably across settings; neither supports a conclusion of equivalence. For health services, symptom outcomes alone tell only part of the story. Future studies should report, by randomized group, who starts treatment, who discontinues it, and who completes the final assessment. These are distinct outcomes that may differ between delivery formats and affect the interpretation of symptom results. Video-based psychotherapy is a reasonable option, but its value should be assessed across the full treatment pathway. Adequately powered noninferiority trials should identify which patients can access, remain in, and benefit from each format.
title: Supporting Video-Based Psychotherapy While Asking Who Benefits and Who Remains in Treatment

summary: PHERGain was a randomized, non-comparative phase 2 trial evaluating a positron 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography (18F-FDG-PET)-guided, pathological complete response (pCR)-adapted strategy to omit chemotherapy in HER2-positive early breast cancer. Female patients with HER2-positive stages I–IIIA operable breast cancer (tumor size ≥ 1.5 cm) were randomized to receive chemotherapy plus trastuzumab and pertuzumab (HP; group A) or HP ± endocrine therapy (group B). In group B, treatment was adapted according to 18F-FDG-PET response after two cycles and pCR, with chemotherapy administered to nonresponders or patients without pCR. We previously reported that this de-escalation approach revealed a 3-year invasive disease-free survival (iDFS) of 94.3% (95% confidence interval (CI): 90.9 to 96.8) in group B. Here we report the prespecified secondary endpoint, 5-year iDFS and exploratory circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) findings. After a median follow-up of 5.6 years, the 5-year iDFS was 89.5% (95% CI: 85.7 to 93.4) in group B (n = 267) and 92.4% (95% CI: 86.7 to 98.5) among 18F-FDG-PET responders achieving pCR without chemotherapy (n = 86), with one distant recurrence. The latter estimate describes a long-term outcome in a post-randomization subgroup defined by 18F-FDG-PET response and pCR and should be interpreted as descriptive rather than as causal effects of omitting chemotherapy. Detectable ctDNA at baseline or during treatment was associated with inferior iDFS, whereas ctDNA clearance correlated with higher pCR rates and improved long-term outcomes. These findings continue to support the clinical validity of an 18F-FDG-PET-guided, pCR-adapted approach and suggest a potential role for ctDNA in refining treatment individualization. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03161353 . A 5-year secondary analysis of the phase 2 PHERGain trial supports the clinical utility of a PET-guided adaptive strategy for treatment de-escalation in HER2-positive early breast cancer and provides circulating tumor DNA insights that could inform further treatment approaches.
title: 5-year outcomes of chemotherapy de-escalation in HER2-positive early breast cancer and exploratory circulating tumor DNA analyses from the randomized phase 2 PHERGain trial

summary: Despite their considerable promise, many current medical foundation models remain modality specific and lack transparent reasoning, limiting clinical adoption. To address this gap, we introduce Explainable Vision Language Foundation Model for Medicine (EVLF-FM), a multimodal vision language foundation model that combines broad diagnostic capabilities with fine-grained explainability. The development and testing of EVLF-FM encompassed more than 1.3 million total samples from 18 global datasets across 10 imaging modalities related to six clinical specialties: dermatology, hepatology, ophthalmology, pathology, pulmonology and radiology. External validation employed 13,443 independent test samples from 17 additional datasets across 10 imaging modalities. EVLF-FM supports disease diagnosis, visual question answering and pixel-level visual grounding with reasoning capabilities. In internal validation for disease diagnostics, EVLF-FM achieved the highest average accuracy, 0.895, outperforming leading generalist and specialist models. In medical visual grounding, EVLF-FM also achieved reasonable performance across nine modalities with average accuracy at 0.5 intersection over union (Acc@0.5) of 0.842. External testing further confirmed consistent zero-shot and few-shot performance, with competitive F1 scores despite a smaller model size. A hybrid training strategy combining supervised and visual reinforcement fine-tuning enables EVLF-FM to generate clinically interpretable explanations aligned with visual evidence. Human evaluation of these reasoning outputs using the S.C.O.R.E. framework yielded a high overall mean score of 4.25/5, supporting their clinical interpretability. Current limitations include the need for additional validation across diverse healthcare settings. Prospective clinical studies are required to evaluate the safety, effectiveness and clinical utility of EVLF-FM before routine clinical deployment. A multimodal vision language foundation model, EVLF-FM, integrates extensive clinical data and advanced training techniques, achieving superior diagnostic accuracy and explainability across diverse imaging modalities, enhancing clinical decision-making through robust reasoning and interpretability.
title: A clinical multimodal vision language foundation model with fine-grain explainability

summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used for text-based emotional support. However, general-purpose LLMs may not consistently recognize emotional cues, adapt supportive strategies to contexts, or generate responses aligned with psychologically informed communication. The limited availability of large-scale, structured Chinese counseling data further constrains the development of models for context-sensitive emotional support. Objective: We developed and evaluated YuanChat, a family of specialized LLMs for context-sensitive emotional support; assessed whether E-URIAL improved response quality; and compared YuanChat with base LLMs. Methods: We constructed 2 datasets from anonymized real-world counseling sessions: ECD-3 (104,897 counselor response turns) for fine-tuning and (9413 manually annotated counselor responses). Annotations covered emotional support conversation stages (exploration, comfort, and action), counseling techniques (clarification, support, and challenge), and empathic effects. We developed 2 YuanChat variants using GLM-4-9B-Chat and Huozi 3.5 as backbone models using parameter-efficient fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We then developed E-URIAL, an inference-time framework combining predicted emotion and support strategy labels with retrieved labeled exemplars. Given the dialogue history through the help seeker’s latest utterance, each model generated a counselor-style response. We compared YuanChat with GPT-4, ERNIE 4.0, CharacterGLM, GLM-4-9B-Chat, and Huozi 3.5. The evaluation comprised (1) automatic evaluation on in-domain and external datasets, assessing empathy identification and empathic expression; (2) evaluation of empathy-related situational reasoning using an expert-developed multiple-choice benchmark; (3) evaluation by clinical experts (n=8) of empathic attunement, support strategy appropriateness, perceived helpfulness, and safety and professional boundary adherence; and (4) a complementary evaluation by volunteer master’s students in clinical and counseling psychology (n=50) of response fluency, empathy, and perceived helpfulness. Results: Fine-tuning increased YuanChat-Huozi3.5’s empathic expression score from 0.57 to 0.68; empathy identification score increased from 0.54 to 0.59. In expert evaluation, YuanChat-Huozi3.5 received a higher empathic attunement score than the base Huozi3.5 model (1.279 vs 0.327; mean difference 0.952, 95% CI 0.746‐1.152). Using professional counselor responses as the reference, the mean differences for YuanChat-Huozi3.5 were 0.148, 0.079, 0.039, and 0.002 in empathic attunement, supportive appropriateness, perceived helpfulness, and safety and professional boundary adherence, respectively. No statistically significant differences were detected between YuanChat-Huozi3.5 and the counselor references (all Holm-adjusted ≥.29). Higher scores were observed when E-URIAL was applied. When E-URIAL was applied with 3 retrieved exemplars, YuanChat-Huozi3.5 achieved an empathy identification score of 0.69 versus 0.59 without E-URIAL, an empathic expression score of 0.79 versus 0.68, and a perceived helpfulness score of 0.74 versus 0.61. Conclusions: The findings indicate that fine-tuning on real-world counseling data and annotating models with structured emotional support labels improved context-sensitive empathic responding in LLMs. Without updating model parameters, E-URIAL further improved empathy identification and empathic expression across multiple models. Together, these methods provide a scalable, theory-informed approach to enhancing the emotional support capabilities of LLMs.
title: A Multistage Fine-Tuning and Empathy Alignment Approach for an Emotional Support Dialogue System: Development and Evaluation Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> AI-enabled patient profiling has been proposed to organize heterogeneous patient data and support personalized nursing care and health support. Given the growing use of AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), digital phenotyping, and digital twins in health care, it is important to clarify how patient profiling has been conceptualized, applied, and evaluated in nursing-relevant contexts. <strong>Objective:</strong> This scoping review aimed to examine and report the available evidence on AI-enabled patient profiling for personalized nursing care and health support. <strong>Methods:</strong> This scoping review was conducted using the Joanna Briggs Institute methodological framework and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews). Chinese and English databases were searched from inception to May 18, 2026, including China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang Data, VIP Database, Chinese Biomedical Literature Database, PubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, and Embase. Eligible studies used AI or computational intelligence methods to construct, classify, apply, validate, or evaluate patient profiles or related patient representations relevant to personalized nursing care or health support. Two reviewers independently screened records, assessed full texts, and charted data using a predefined form. Data were synthesized descriptively and narratively using an input-process-output framework. <strong>Results:</strong> A total of 61 studies were included. AI-enabled patient profiling was represented through patient profiles, patient or user personas, digital phenotypes, patient segments, clinical subtypes, digital twins, and LLM-enabled personalization. Included studies used diverse data sources, including electronic health records, nursing records, patient-reported outcomes, questionnaires, mobile app data, wearable and sensor data, engagement logs, and textual or conversational data. Common AI approaches included machine learning, clustering, deep learning, natural language processing, recommender systems, knowledge graphs, digital twin modeling, and LLMs. Applications focused on personalized education, self-management support, rehabilitation, chronic disease management, remote monitoring, decision support, follow-up care, and shared decision-making. Most studies evaluated algorithmic performance, feasibility, usability, or system development, whereas fewer studies examined profile validity, actionability, equity, workflow integration, or long-term nursing-sensitive and patient-centered outcomes. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Existing evidence positions AI-enabled patient profiling as an emerging data-to-action mechanism for personalized nursing care and health support rather than as a mature clinical intervention. Future research should strengthen conceptual clarity, validate the profile, establish explicit pathways linking profiles to actions, incorporate nurse and patient involvement, assess equity and safety, and evaluate implementation in real-world nursing settings. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong> OSF Registry mey4u; https://osf.io/mey4u
title: AI-Enabled Patient Profiling for Personalized Nursing Care and Health Support: Scoping Review

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Digital health technologies are transforming health care by improving access, efficiency, and quality of care. However, recent studies highlight that digitalization can unintentionally reinforce or deepen existing social and health inequalities, as not all population groups benefit equally from digital progress. The concept of digital determinants of health (DDoH) has emerged to better capture how digital factors shape health opportunities and outcomes. The systematic incorporation of DDoH and other health determinants shaped by digitalization into strategic planning remains limited. As a result, health systems may lack structured approaches to identify them and anticipate their equity implications. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to identify which health determinants are considered most important in the Catalan context and to qualitatively explore their inclusion in existing regional strategies and policy frameworks in Catalonia. <strong>Methods:</strong> We conducted a modified Delphi study with experts from the Catalan health and digital ecosystem. The list of determinants was derived from a scoping review, which identified 127 determinants that emerged or changed with digitalization. Experts living and working in Catalonia, with experience in digital health, public health, health care delivery, social or DDoH, or health equity, were recruited using snowball sampling. Participants rated each determinant for importance using a 5-point Likert scale across 2 rounds, followed by a final online consensus meeting. For each determinant, the median (IQR) and the proportion of experts rating it as 4 or 5 were calculated, and items were classified into high, moderate, or low relevance according to predefined consensus criteria. <strong>Results:</strong> A total of 43 experts participated in the first Delphi round, and 31 completed the second round. Of the 127 assessed determinants, 20 (15.7%) reached high relevance for the Catalan context, including 15 digital, 4 social, and 1 political determinant. Overall, the most important determinants focused on enabling the effective and equitable use of digital health, particularly access, skills, system-level digital capacity and governance, inclusive design, and the responsible use of AI. Comparison with the original global Delphi study showed substantial overlap, but also revealed context-specific priorities. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> This study demonstrates the value of systematically contextualizing DDoH and other health determinants shaped by digitalization to inform strategic health planning in digitally mature public health systems. The findings show that international digital health agendas require regional reprioritization to reflect local infrastructure, governance arrangements and equity challenges. The results suggest that, beyond technological capacity, governance and equity considerations should become central to digital health planning. The proposed approach offers a replicable framework to support more anticipatory, coordinated and equity-oriented digital health strategies.
title: Assessing Digital Determinants of Health and Their Impact as Part of Strategic Health Planning in Catalonia: Modified Delphi Study

summary: Background: Electronic health record–derived process measures such as vital-sign record density are used for quality monitoring, risk prediction, and cross-system benchmarking, but whether they retain consistent meaning across sites and data streams is rarely tested. Objective: This study aimed to determine whether vital-sign record density varies primarily by data stream, database, contributing site, or care unit, and what follows for comparative use. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) version 3.1 and the eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD) version 2.0. Record density and timing metrics were computed for the first 24 intensive care unit hours from nurse-charted streams and, in eICU-CRD, from the monitor stream. Heart rate was primary; oxygen saturation and respiratory rate were replication variables. Variance was decomposed by database, hospital, and unit using η2 with hospital-clustered bootstrap inference and mixed-effects sensitivity analyses. A hospital-level plausibility floor of 12 nurse-charted heart rate observations per 24 hours was applied for the principal analysis; unrestricted and alternative-floor analyses are reported as sensitivities. Results: A pooled-item MIMIC-IV heart rate count included alarm-limit documentation events, so label-based pooling mixes the two. In 117,572 eICU-CRD stays present in both streams, nurse- and monitor-derived counts were almost unrelated (Spearman ρ=0.024), with bottom-decile overlap at chance. Between-database η2 for record count was 0.960 against the eICU monitor stream and 0.026 against the nurse stream. Eight of 68 eICU-CRD hospitals fell below the plausibility floor and were excluded from principal estimates, a restriction introduced during review. Among the remaining 60 hospitals (88,560 stays), hospital η2 for record count was 0.354 (95% CI 0.259-0.450) against unit-within-hospital η2 of 0.043; for the interval-structure metrics, the hospital and unit components were not separable. For record count, the hospital component fell from 0.441 unrestricted to 0.321 at an hourly floor. A negative-binomial mixed model gave latent-scale hospital and unit variance-partition coefficients of 0.348 (95% CI 0.252-0.457) and 0.112 (0.078-0.163), equivalent to 0.318 and 0.110 observed. A pooled bottom-decile rule agreed with hospital-specific rules on 52.5% (4726/9006) of flagged stays, with 6 hospitals supplying half the pooled decile. The hospital component for record count replicated at 0.322 for oxygen saturation and 0.333 for respiratory rate. Conclusions: Within a multisite nurse-charted stream, vital-sign record volume varied more across contributing sites than across care units within hospitals; for the interval-structure metrics, the site and unit components were not separable at this cohort size. Apparent cross-database differences were reproduced by source-table choice, and site-level variation remained after excluding the most evident contribution-completeness outliers. Comparative use therefore requires specifying the generating stream, enforcing the analytic window, and explicitly modeling site-level variation; the residual site component should not be interpreted as documentation practice alone.
title: Data Stream and Hospital-Level Variation in Intensive Care Unit Vital-Sign Record Density Across Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV and eICU Collaborative Research Database: Retrospective Data Quality Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Digital health interventions, including mobile health apps, increasingly complement outpatient mental health care. In Germany, certified digital health applications (DiGA [Digitale Gesundheitsanwendungen]) can be prescribed and reimbursed in the statutory health care system. However, real-world evidence on patient-reported use of DiGA for mental disorders remains limited. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to analyze usage patterns and experiences among DiGA users and expectations among nonusers. Among users, we examined duration of active use, self-reported completion, and experienced reasons for discontinuation; among nonusers, whether DiGA use would be an option and the perceived relevance of hypothetical reasons for discontinuation. <strong>Methods:</strong> We conducted an anonymous cross-sectional mixed-mode survey among adults insured by Techniker Krankenkasse, Germany’s largest statutory insurer. Random samples of 2000 individuals per group were invited in April 2024, and data collection ended in September 2024. Users received an activation code for a DiGA authorized for mental disorders. Nonusers had a documented diagnosis for which a DiGA was available but had no prior use. Analyses were descriptive, using available cases, frequencies, and medians with IQRs for ordinal Likert-type items. Actual and intended use were treated as distinct. Exploratory subgroup analyses were conducted. <strong>Results:</strong> Overall, 1413 participants were included in the analysis (769 of 2000 invited users; 644 of 2000 invited nonusers), with response rates of 38.5% (95% CI 36.3%-40.6%) and 32.2% (95% CI 30.2%-34.3%), respectively. A total of 840 of 1249 (67.3%; 95% CI 64.6%-69.8%) participants were female. Nonusers were older and more often lived in rural areas. Among users, 487 of 687 (70.9%; 95% CI 67.4%-74.2%) reported active use for at least 5 weeks; 409 of 700 (58.4%; 95% CI 54.7%-62.0%) reported completion of their DiGA program. The proportion of reported completions increased from 111 of 250 (44.4%; 95% CI 38.4%-50.6%) among those aged 18-40 years to 85 of 112 (75.9%; 95% CI 67.2%-82.9%) among those aged 61 years and older. The most frequently endorsed reasons for discontinuation among users reporting noncompletion were lack of motivation (151/272, 55.5%; 95% CI 49.6%-61.3%) and insufficient personalization (114/255, 44.7%; 95% CI 38.7%-50.8%). Among nonusers, the most frequently endorsed hypothetical reasons for discontinuation were mismatch with their condition (431/540, 79.8%; 95% CI 76.2%-83.0%) and technical difficulties (432/545, 79.3%; 95% CI 75.7%-82.5%). <strong>Conclusions:</strong> This study provides patient-reported real-world evidence on certified and reimbursable digital mental health interventions. Many users reported weeks of active use, but noncompletion remained common and was more frequent among younger users. Lack of motivation as a frequently reported reason for discontinuation suggests that supporting continued engagement may be important during DiGA use. Beyond Germany, these findings may support implementation of digital mental health interventions in other health care systems. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong>
title: Digital Health Applications for Mental Disorders in Germany Among Users and Nonusers on Actual and Intended Use, Self-Reported Completion, and Reasons for Discontinuation: Cross-Sectional Survey

summary: Background: Emerging evidence indicates that immersive virtual reality can be used therapeutically and has demonstrated efficacy in promoting the mental health of older adults. Nevertheless, there remains a paucity of qualitative research examining the specific experiences underpinning these benefits. Objective: This study aimed to explore the perspectives of older adults who received the 12-session Immersive Virtual Reality Therapeutic Programme (IVRTP) intervention and health-related undergraduate students who delivered it as interventionists, within the context of residential care homes. Methods: A descriptive qualitative study was conducted as a qualitative exploration embedded in a multicenter randomized controlled trial evaluating the effects of IVRTP in promoting the mental health of older adults with disabilities living in residential homes. The IVRTP incorporated therapeutic elements of tourism, natural scenes, and reminiscence. Data were collected through focus group interviews and analyzed using thematic analysis. Results: Seven groups of older adults (n=28) and 3 groups of student interventionists (n=9) participated in the study. Five themes emerged: IVRTP contributes to “broadening horizons” through embracing new technology, learning new things, and engaging in new activities. Participants noted that the IVRTP provided “a realistic journey and immersive escape” from their residential home environment and mobility issues. They expressed that the IVRTP evoked “reminiscent memories” from the past and were amazed at the observed changes in tourist destinations over time. The interviews were filled with laughter and affirmations of positive emotions associated with this “joyful adventure,” although a few participants mentioned “minor discomfort,” such as eye soreness and dizziness, from wearing the head-mounted devices. Students’ accounts corroborated these themes; their meaning-making and colearning with older adults underscored the pedagogical value of authentic, community-based, intergenerational learning and reinforced the case for integrating a community practicum into the curriculum. Conclusions: Implementing an IVRTP in residential care settings, particularly for older adults with mobility limitations, is positively viewed as an accessible, enjoyable, and beneficial intervention to support psychosocial well-being. Therapeutically oriented content delivered through a structured protocol, coupled with the use of advanced IVR technology, was appreciated by both older adults and student interventionists.
title: Experiences of Immersive Virtual Reality Among Older Adults With Physical Disabilities: Qualitative Process Evaluation of a Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial

summary: Background: Addressing the burnout epidemic among health care providers remains one of the foremost challenges of modern health care systems. Past researchers have turned to passively gathered biometric data from wearable devices to identify key variables that predict burnout. However, this has resulted in limited success. Objective: This pilot and feasibility study aimed to test the feasibility and accuracy of developing an Extreme Gradient Boosting machine learning model to classify health care providers as being at higher or lower risk of burnout based on their biometric data. Methods: We conducted a 3-month pilot and feasibility study where health care providers self-reported burnout every 6 weeks and wore a Garmin Venu 3 smartwatch to collect continuous biometric data. Participants were recruited from 3 pediatric urgent care sites and an inpatient hospitalist division of a pediatric health care system. We had a final sample of 41 participants who met our inclusion criteria requiring completion of burnout measurements at 2 of the 3 time points and having worn the watch for at least 70% of the study period. Participants were asked to wear the Garmin watch continuously over the course of the study. Burnout self-report surveys were delivered via email. Our main outcome was burnout as measured using the Maslach Burnout Inventory–Human Services Survey. The measure consists of 3 subscales that together constitute burnout: emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and reduced personal efficacy. Results: First, we found evidence of feasibility for wearable watches to be used in situ for health care providers to gather data passively for the purposes of classifying burnout. A total of 82% (51/62) of participants met our criteria of wearing the watch 70% of the time, with 66% (41/62) having corresponding burnout scores to be included in analyses. Second, our machine learning model achieved strong overall performance in identifying risk of burnout, with strong sensitivity and specificity, demonstrating that biometric data collected using wearable devices can accurately predict burnout. Conclusions: Our evidence of feasibility offers promising results for a passive method of data collection to be used for classifying burnout risk in other health care settings. Furthermore, the strong performance of our machine learning model provides a foundational step toward improving an organization’s ability to respond and mitigate burnout through thoughtful intervention strategies.
title: Identifying Burnout in Pediatric Clinicians Using Wearable Biometric Data: Development and Feasibility Study

summary: The incidence of early-onset colorectal cancer (EO-CRC; diagnosed before age 50 years) is increasing worldwide. Although current data indicate that EO-CRC may be biologically distinct from average-onset CRC (AO-CRC; diagnosed at age ≥50 years), molecular differences remain poorly defined. To address this knowledge gap, we generated a single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) atlas from 189 primary CRC tumors (54 EO-CRC, 135 AO-CRC) spanning eight decades of life, with at least 20 tumors in most age decades. Our analyses stratified tumors by microsatellite status and accounted for tumor sidedness, stage, patient sex and neoadjuvant treatment history, modeling age continuously or categorically (EO-CRC versus AO-CRC). Among microsatellite-stable (MSS) tumors, those from younger patients were characterized by increased stromal and decreased epithelial proportions, which we confirmed using multispectral immunofluorescence and machine learning in an external cohort of 712 MSS CRC tumors (18 EO-CRC, 694 AO-CRC). Tumor epithelial cells from young patients exhibited increased expression of long noncoding RNAs and FN1, with a trend toward increased heterogeneity in copy number alterations. MSS left-sided EO-CRC tumors had more cell–cell interactions, with epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition-related signaling pathways (FN1/GDF/ACTIVIN) showing increased, cell type-specific interactions. Our large high-resolution snRNA-seq atlas uncovers age-associated features of CRC and provides a resource for the community to understand EO-CRC biology. A high-resolution snRNA-seq atlas of 189 colorectal tumors from patients aged 20–90+ years uncovers age-associated features of colorectal cancer.
title: Insights into early-onset colorectal cancer from a single-nucleus RNA-seq atlas of colorectal cancer across the age continuum

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Medication nonadherence remains a major global health challenge, contributing to preventable disease, hospitalizations, and health care costs. Mobile health (mHealth) apps incorporating gamification and financial incentives have shown potential to improve adherence; however, most research has focused on patient perspectives, with limited understanding of how nonpatient stakeholders perceive their feasibility, risks, and implementation. Understanding nonpatient stakeholder perspectives in relation to patient viewpoints is essential for informing future policy development and establishing practical, industry-supported safeguards that protect consumers while enabling innovation. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to explore nonpatient stakeholder perspectives on the use of gamification and financial incentives in mHealth apps for medication adherence and to inform consensus-based design and policy considerations. <strong>Methods:</strong> A study was conducted using a modified virtual nominal group technique (vNGT). Nonpatient stakeholders across health care, industry, and policy sectors in Australia were recruited through purposive and convenience sampling between February and August 2025. Data collection involved a survey capturing demographics and initial perspectives, followed by online focus groups for consensus discussions. Qualitative responses were analyzed using thematic analysis supported by AI-assisted coding. Consensus statements derived from themes were rated during the focus groups. Additional probing prompts were used in the focus groups to encourage further discussion where consensus was not immediately achieved. Results from the focus groups were analyzed using descriptive statistics to summarize consensus ratings and discussions. <strong>Results:</strong> A total of 20 participants were included in the study. Nine participants reported having a health care professional background employment exclusively, while 11 reported having employment background across multiple sectors or exclusively outside health care. Six key themes were identified: tailored gamification for adherence, financial incentives as a contested motivator, designing for diversity and inclusion, usability barriers to engagement, trust through data governance, and validated and sustainable innovation. These informed 24 consensus statements, of which 54% (13/24) achieved unanimous agreement. Stakeholders strongly endorsed personalization, simplicity, and transparent data practices, while expressing nuanced concerns regarding the ethical use, sustainability, and potential unintended consequences of financial incentives. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Nonpatient stakeholders largely reinforce patient priorities while extending them with critical perspectives on implementation, governance, and sustainability. Gamification and financial incentives are viewed as potentially effective but require careful, ethically grounded design to balance engagement with long-term motivation and trust. These findings support the development of stakeholder-informed guidelines for responsible mHealth innovation and highlight the importance of integrating patient and system-level perspectives in digital health design. Future research should prioritize co-designed longitudinal studies using apps with gamification and a range of incentive offers with clear redemption processes to evaluate the long-term impact on medication adherence across diverse patient populations.
title: Nonpatient Stakeholder Perspectives on the Use of Gamification and Financial Incentives in Mobile Health for Medication Adherence: Modified Nominal Group Technique Study

summary: After spinal cord injury, clinical management aims to support tissue perfusion, but current methods rely on the indirect control of arterial blood pressure without direct measurement of the local blood flow. This limits the ability to tailor drug delivery to the injured tissue. Here, we show that spinal cord blood flow can be regulated using a closed-loop controller that adjusts vasopressor infusion on the basis of real-time ultrasound flow measurement. We characterize the dynamic relationship between drug infusion, arterial pressure and spinal cord blood flow, and we use these data to design a feedback controller that targets a predefined flow level. We validate the system in simulations, implement the controller in real time in rodents and translate it to pigs. We show that the controller reduced blood flow deviations and variability compared with constant dosing and supported functional recovery in a rodent survival model. These results show a closed-loop spinal cord perfusion control strategy that leverages clinically available measurements and pharmacological interventions, supporting its translation to clinical settings for the management of acute spinal cord injury. A closed-loop control strategy regulates spinal cord blood flow by adjusting norepinephrine infusion using real-time flow measurements, enabling direct flow targeting after acute injury.
title: Optimal closed-loop feedback control of blood flow after spinal cord injury with norepinephrine

summary: Background: AI is a broad field encompassing various techniques, which include algorithms that learn from data to perform automated tasks without explicit human programming. Public health aims to protect and improve the health of communities and populations at the local, regional, national, and global levels, but it typically has limited resources. While AI may lead to improved efficiency or effectiveness of public health interventions, the adoption of AI interventions should be informed by evidence of effective use in practice. Objective: This review aims to summarize how AI-assisted interventions are currently used by public health professionals. Methods: We conducted a scoping review to identify the current uses of AI in public health. We searched MEDLINE (Ovid), Embase (Ovid), Web of Science (Core Collection), and Scopus for relevant reports published between January 1, 2020, and July 24, 2025. Two reviewers independently screened reports. Eligible reports were primary studies (experimental or observational), commentaries, and editorials that discussed how AI tools have been used in practice in public health contexts relevant to high-income countries, excluding outbreaks. Data were extracted by one reviewer and checked by a second. Results: We screened 5400 records and 155 full texts, including 8 reports. These reports discussed a variety of uses of AI tools across public health domains: 3 reports used chatbots in different settings, 1 report used machine learning to forecast health service demand, 2 reports used AI for symptom checking, and 2 reports used AI for evidence synthesis. While assessing the effectiveness of AI tools for public health was beyond the scope of this review, and most reports did not robustly evaluate effectiveness, the evidence for the effectiveness of AI tools was nonetheless mixed. One report described a chatbot that users found helpful, while another found a specific chatbot to be ineffective, highlighting its potential to undermine trust in the organization that developed it. Another report highlighted both benefits and drawbacks of a large language model used to communicate with socially isolated individuals. The main finding of this review was that even with a comprehensive search across multiple databases, there were few reports of how AI tools are being used in practice in public health contexts. Conclusions: The lack of evidence from public health practice, excluding outbreaks, makes it difficult to know which uses of AI, if any, would be useful to incorporate into practice in high-income countries. In the absence of evidence, new interventions, including those using AI, should be evaluated to ensure they are effective (and cost-effective). These evaluations should be widely and accessibly disseminated to create an evidence base that other public health teams could use to inform their own decisions around AI tools.
title: The Current Roles of AI in Public Health Practice: Scoping Review
